Actual Transformation of Sentient Beings into rocks and stones {174); Site of some
long-past remarkable occurrence {175-176).

171. The belief on the part of the Indians in the presence of Mountain Spirits in certain locahties would seem to have been due in large
measure to one or another of three sets of causes: peculiarities in
conformation, marking, position, and other features of the rocks
(on the principle of suiting a picture to the frame) ; the supposed
transformation of the person or animal into stone; or the association
of the locahty with some remarkable event that took place in the
long-ago.

There are an endless number and variety of Spirits connected with
mountains, precipices, rocks, cataracts, etc. (cf. Sect. 68). South of
the Takutu River is a mountain chain taking its name from a hill
resembling a crescent in the distance, whence the Wapisianas have
compared it to the moon (Kaira in their language), and designating it
in consequence Kai-irite, or Mountains of the Moon (ScT, 48) . Now
all this country in Schomburgk's time was terra incognita to both
Brazilians and Indians, and hence, as might have been expected, and
as he tells us, "the Indian banishes all evil spirits 'to this region,
while the Brazilian considers it the abode of wild Indians who massacre
any person foolhardy enough to come within their precincts." So
extraordinarily has nature molded her mountain forms in different
parts of the Guianas, that there are seldom wanting resemblances,
comparatively striking, to common everyday objects. I can quite
ssrmpathize with Schomburgk when he so much regretted that the
little knowledge which he possessed of the Makusi language did not
permit him to understand some of the many wonderful stories the
Indians had to tell him of every stone they met on the road that was
of more than ordinary size or fantastically shaped by nature (ScF,
199). Along the valley of the Unamara, a very good example is
Mara-etshiba, the highest mountain, where the bulgmg out in the
middle of this mass of rock has been identified with the maraka.
Another is Mount Canu-yeh-piapa (Ht. "guava-tree stump"), while
a third is Mount Pur6-piapa ("headless tree") (ScF, 197). Elsewhere, there is Mount Pakaraima, a singular isolated mountain
which from its figure "has been called the Pakara or Pakal, meaning

236 ANIMISM AND FOLK-LOSE OF GUIANA INDIANS [bth. ann. 30

a basket" (ScF, 221). Mount Sororieng, the "swallows' nest," an
object of mucli dread to the superstitious, is another good instance
" (BW, 177). The Takwiari offset of the Twasinkie Mountains, Essequibo, derives its Carib name from a remarkable pile of large granite
bowlders so placed as to resemble a water-jar, called Comuti by the
Arawak Indians, and by this name they are more commonly known
(ScR, I, 328). Ayangcanna Mountain can be seen in the distance
from the upper Mazaruni, forming a most singular picture. The
word means "hce-searchers," this disagreeable name being bestowed
on account of a row of huge pointed rocks on the crest, which are
sharply defined against the sky, and to the Indian eye resemble a
row of women seated one behind the other, searching each other'p
head for vermin, a custom very prevalent among all Guiana tribes
(Bro, 390). It must be admitted that such fancied resemblances are
not always too clear to European eyes. Clear or not, however, once
the resemblance admitted, then follow the explanation and the
"padding," the pointing of the so-called moral to adorn the tale.
Wayaca-piapa Mountain, northwest of Roraima, is the "felled tree"
which, as the Indians say, the Spirit Makonaima cut down duringhis journey through these parts. On the Mazaruni, near Masanassa
village, relates Boddam-Whetham : "We passed a peculiar rock in
the middle of the river somewhat resembling a htmaan figure: the
Indians thought it was a river-god watching for pacu" (BW, 179).
On some granite blocks, above the Waraputa Rapids, Essequibo
River, "I found," says Schomburgk, "two impressions of a man's
foot, as if he had sprung from one rock to the other. The imprint
of each foot, even to that of the five toes, was really striking. The
Indians told us that these were the tracks which the Great Spirit had
left behind when he took his departure along this route from among
their forefathers with whom he used to live" (ScR, i, 326).

In passing the Caro-miring [branch oi the upper Mazaruni] the guide informed us
that when high it is navigable for canoes for half a day's journey up, to the foot of a
high fall, at which there is a large sand-beach, marked with mysterious footprints
resembling those made by the human foot. The sand also is thrown up as if children
had been playing there. If the Indians who visit the spot trample down these heaps,
and go away for a short time, on their return they find them there again as before.
The Indians believe that wild men live near the spot, but have never succeeded in
seeing them. [Bro, 385.]

The torrential streams which so suddenly gush down from the
heights of Roraima are but the sorrowful tears of the Mother of Pia
and Makonaima — she who had been left behind on top of this mountain by the former (Da, 342). At least that is what the Makusis
affirm. Some people say that over the tops of Roraima and Kukenam
are spread seas fDled with all kinds of fish, especially dolphins, and
continually circlsd by gigantic white eagles, which act as perpetual
watchmen (ScR, ii, 265)."

THIRTIETH ANNUAL REPORT PLATE 4

THE KAIETEUR FALL

(From D. photograph by W. 11. McTurk)

172. Another example of this series of cases is the legend relative
to the celebrated Kaieteur,Fall (pi. 4), which I give here in the words
of Barrington Brown (Bro, 214), the discoverer of this wonder-spot:

-Once upon a time there was a large village above the fall, situated on the little
savanna, amongst the inhabitants of which was an old Indian, who had arrived at
that period of human existence, when his life had become a burden to himself and a
trouble to his relatives. Amongst other duties, there devolved upon his near relations the tedious one o! extracting the jiggers from his toes which there accumulated
day by day. These duties becoming irksome at last, it was arranged that the old
man should be assisted on his way to his long home, that spirit land hdng two-days'
journey beyond the setting sun. He was accordingly transferred, with his pegall of
worldly goods, from his house to a woodskin on the river above the head of the great
fall, and launched forth upon the stream. The silent flood bore him to its brink,
where the rushing waters received him in their deadly grasp, bearing his enfeebled
body down to its watery grave in the basin below. Not long after, strange to relate,
his woodskin appeared in the form of a pointed rock, which to this day is seen not
far from our lower barometer station; while on the sloping mass of talus to the west of
the basin, a huge square rock is said to be his petrified pegall or canister. Thus has
the fall been named Kaieteur in memory of the victim of this tragic event.

173. The remarkable petroglyphs, scattered through the Guianas,
to which so many travelers have drawn attention, are in the same
way credited with a supernatural origin. Thus Schomburgk rslates,
when at the Waraputa Rapids: "I was most anxious to carry away
part of one of the rocks . . . and neither threats nor promises could
induce any of our Indians to strike a blow against these monuments
of their ancestors' skill and superiority. They ascribe them to the
Great Spirit, and their existence was known to all the tribes met with.
The greatest uneasiness was depicted upon the faces of our poor crew;
in the very abode of the Spirits, they momentarily expected to see
fire descend to punish our temerity" (ScG, 275). The Piapocos of
the lower Guaviar River ascribe such rock-gravings to their Maminaimis, or Water Spirits (Cr, 525, 529) . The amount of intelligence
displayed by the expression of such a behef was however, within comparatively recent times, paralleled by that of a European Power, for
on the Montagne d' Argent on the coast between Cayenne and the
River Oyapock, the rock-carvings were claimed by the Portuguese
to represent the coat-of-arms of Charles V when they had a dispute
with the French over their boundary line (Cr, 145).

174. The existence has been shown (Sect. 58) of a belief in the
origin of human and animal life from rocks or stones and in the transformation of such sentient beings into the inorganic material similar to
that from which they have sprung. This transformation is regarded
not only as a natural departure from the normal covirse of events, but
also in the light of a pimishment (Sect. 67). At Aramayka, a settlement on the Mazaruni, close to Karamang River, the cliffs of Marabiacru become visible to the height of about one thousand feet, with
perpendicular faces on the north. A remarkable detached peaked

238 ANIMISM AND FOLK-LOEE OF GUIANA INDIANS [eth. ANN. SO

rock on the western face of the cliffs is called the Caribisce. The
legend says it is a man of that nation turned into stone for attempting
to scale the cliff (HiA, 32). The Nation of Stone-adzes, where all the
people are really stones, has been mentioned (Sect. 158). But however produced, these inorganic objects with human instincts, powers,
and ideas, so to speak, aU play a more or less important part on the
world's stage. Thus, a rugged rock, a real good, friend, comes and
quells the fountain which threatens to OTerwhelm the nation (BrB,
106). In those cases in which the transformation is the result of
pimishment it might only be expected that the propensities of such
rocks and stones would be directed into channels other than good.
Perhaps it was some idea similar to this which led to the loss of
Schomburgk's geological specimens: "One of the Indian carriers
said he had lost my geological specimens : my brother had previously
warned me of this — the Indian thinks it something evil, and wUl
secretly throw it away" (ScR, i, 433). The same may possibly be
said of the following: Above the cataracts of the River Demerary
, are abvmdance of red and white agates, which remain untouched by
the natives, who avoid them from a principle of superstitious veneration) as they are dedicated to the service of their magical invocations
(Ba, 21). Probably some idea of this nature may form the basis of
the practice noted by BroAvn, in the Cotinga District, in connection
with certain small artificial stone-heaps on the sides of the paths
over the Savannah Mountains. These were 3 or 4 feet in height.
The Indians with him, in passing, had added to the heaps by dropping
on them stones picked up near by; he could never learn their object
in so doing, for when questioned about it, they only laughed (Bro,
276). (In the Gran Chaco, the Indians, on going over a pass, will
place a stone on the ground, so that they will not get tired on the
way (Nor, 12).)"

The Indians have a tradition\nthat the cliffs, hillocks, and other places, about a mUe from Kayiwa on\nthe Corentyne are inhabited by a large snake, which from time to time\ngoes to drink the water of the river, and that its passage thither has\ndeprived the cliffs of vegetation (ScC, 289). On a low hill above the\nWaiquah River, a branch of the Cotinga, Barrington Brown \"observed a huge artificial mound of earth and small stones, which the\nguide said was the grave of Makunaima's brother. It would seem that\nthe Great Spirit is a dweller in this region, for an isolated rocky mountain, seen from the Cotinga lower down, at the head of the Mauitzie\nRiver, is called Makunaima-outa, which means the 'Great Spirit's\nHouse'\" (Bro,276). In the Pakaraima Mountains there is a singular\nrockcalled by the Makusis Toupanaghoe, from its resemblance to ahand.\nThe Indians make it the seat of a demon and pass it imder fear and\ntrembling (ScG, 256). At the Merume escarpment, upper Mazaruni,\nsays Brown, ' ' the Indians begged my men not to roast salt fish on the\nembers, fearing thereby to rouse the ire of a large eagle and camoodie\nsnake, which they said lived on the moimtain side, and would show\ntheir displeasure by causing more rain to fall\" (Bro, 399). According\nto the tale told by a medicine-man. Mount Roraima was guarded by\nan enormous camudi, which could entwine a hundred people in its\nfolds. He himself had once approached its den and had seen demons\nrunning about as numerous as quails (BW, 225). Another Indian\nin the same neighborhood objected to camping near what he believed\nto be the cave of a celebrated \"water-mama,\" near which it was\ndangerous to sleep (BW, 210).\n\n176. Sometimes the facts of the original occurrence have been lost\nsight of and only a memory remains, but this memory is grafted on\nthe minds of the Indians apparently in the form of a Spirit, if we are\nto judge by the procedures adopted on their visiting such localities —\nthese must neither be approached too closely, nor pointed to, and\nsometimes not even looked at, or spoken of. Although it is permissible to single out a person by a nod with the head, to point the\nfinger at a fellow-creature is to offer him as serious an affront as it\nwould be to step over him when he is lying on the ground (Sect. 72);\nin the latter case he would tell you that he is not dead yet, and that\nyou must wait until he is. To point the finger at a Spirit must\nnecessarily be a much more serious matter. We have the Old Man's\nRock in the Essequibo, which a murdered buckeen continually\nhaunts, and at which it is dangerous to point the finger (A, i, 93).\nSo also, there is a large bare rock (the Negro Cap) standing with its\nhead about six feet above the water, close to the Three Brothers\nIslands, in the same river, concerning which the natives entertain a\nmost curious superstition. They believe that if any individual\npoints at this rock a heavy storm will immediately overtake him for\nhis audacity (StC, ii, 37). The dangers consequent upon talking\nabout Spirits have already been dealt with (Sect. 1^4)) hence the\nfollowing allusion from im Thurn is of interest: \"In very dry seasons,\nwhen the water in the riA^ers is low, the rocks in their beds are seen to\nhave a curious glazed, vitrified and black appearance, due probably\n\n240 ANIMISM AND FOLK-LORE OP GUIANA INDIANS [bth.ann.30\n\nto deposits of iron and manganese. Whenever I questioned the\nIndians about these rocks, I was at once silenced by the assertion\nthat any allusion to their appearance would vex these rocks and\ncause them to send misfortune\" (IT, 354). The most curious, however, of all the procedures indicative of a Spirit's presence somewhere\nin the immediate neighborhood is that which concerns the sense of\nsight; several examples of this temporary occlusion of vision are\n-recorded elsewhere (Sect. i52).\n\nChapteb xn"
}

  "passage_text": "THE SPIRITS OF THE WATER\n\nNames and general appearance: Anthropomorphic (777) ; partly human, partly animal {178); Zoomorphic, as porpoise, manati, macaw (i79), snake {180), big fish, Omar\n{181-182) ; derived from men or animals {183) ; kindly disposed on the whole — they\ngave man his water-jug and potato {184), the rattle and tobacco {185); of an amorous\ndisposition {186-187), with strong likings for menstruating women {188-189) ; share, with\nBush Spirits, the responsibility for sickness, accident, and death (190) ; responsible\nalso for the Tidal Wave {191); they object to mention of their names and antecedents\n{191); to a pot-spoon being washed outside the traveling boat {19S); and woe betide\nthe voyager if he dares to utter certain forbidden words {194)-\n\n177. The Water Spirits, whether anthropomorphic or zoomorphic,\nare known as Ori-yu or Orehu (Arawak), Ho-ardnni (Warrau), Okoyumo (Carib), etc. The Warraus, especially a swamp-inhabiting\ntribe, seem to have made several distinctions in their Spirits: they\nhad their Ahdba, Ho-inarau or Ho-ardnni, and Xaba-rau or Xabaranni. The Ahtiba is the \"Fish-mamma,\" the chief of all the fish —\none male and one female. The two hve in imdergroimd water; their\nheads are hke those of people, but their bodies resemble those of\nfish though they are provided with all the different kinds of feet\nbelonging to land animals. They work evil on mankind ; when shipwreck takes place they eat the bodies. The Ho-inarau and Xabarau represent the Water Spirits of the sea and the rivers, respectively; they are sometimes hke people, sometimes Uke fish, and\nwere once good and kind, but the Warraus have made them bad.\nIndeed, there was a time when these Water People used to hve in\namity and friendship with the Land People. There are two reasons\nfor the termination of this ideal state of existence. The Warraus\nused to exchange wives with them in those days, that is, a wife would\nbe taken as required alternately from the one and the other tribe\n(see Sect. 190). The Warrau supply ran short, however, and the\nWater Spirits accordingly became vexed and angered with them.\nThe second alleged reason is that the Warraus insisted on the isolation\nof the women at their menstrual periods, a practice to which the\nWater Spirits were unaccustomed and strongly objected (Sect. 190).\nThough some of the Water Spirits have been repeatedly described\nby certain authors as the Water-mamma, they have nothing whatever\nto do with the African-Creole superstition represented under that\ndesignation. Still less have they necessarily any connection with\nthe water-cow or manati (the Km-u-moro of the Arawaks), or with\nthe water-camudi (the madre del agua of the old Spanish authors),\n\n15961° — 30BTH— 15 16 241\n\n242 ANIMISM AND FOLK-LOBE OP GUIANA INDIANS [eth. ann. 30\n\nexcept of course in the possibility that the physical attributes and\npeculiarities of these and other huge creatures have had to be\naccounted for in the Indian cosmogony. The natives of the Amazons\ncountry have their mai d'agoa — ^Mother or Spirit of the Water — ^in\nthe shape of a water serpent said to be many score fathoms in length,\na monster doubtless suggested by the occasional appearance of the\nanaconda {Eunectes murinus), which assumes a great variety of\nforms (HWB, 236). One of the many mysterious tales told of the\nBouto, as the large dolphin of the Amazons is called, \"was to, the\neffect that a Bouto once had the habit of assuming the shape of a\nbeautiful woman, with hair hanging loose to her heels, and walking\nashore at night in the streets of Ega to entice the young men down to\nthe water. If anyone was so much smitten as to follow her to the\nwater-side, she grasped her victim round the waist and plunged\nbeneath the waves with a triumphant cry\" (HWB, 309).\n\nThe accounts of these Water Folk vary a great deal, but I believe\nthe following represents the consensus of Arawak opinion. The\nOriyus always Hve in the water and one at least accompanies every\ncorial. If an accident takes place the Spirit is blamed for it. These\nSpirits may appear in human shape, impersonating both sexes.\nThe female sometimes can be seen bathing on the banks of a stream,\nor combing her long hair with a silver comb, which she occasionally\nforgets and leaves behind in her hurry to return to the water when\nsuddenly surprised. '"

  "passage_text": "178. Oriyu sometimes splashes and tramples the water like a horse
where horses are known not to exist; Brett even goes so far as to teU
us that "she sometimes presents herself above the water with the
head of a horse or other animal as it may suit her fancy, or the object
she has in view" (Br, 367). On the other hand, I have often heard
her or him described by Warraus as having a fish's head. Brett as a
matter of fact always speaks of Oriyu as a female. Of remaining
Water People those mentioned by im Thurn as the Huroni (cf. the
Warrau term Ho-ardnni, Water Spirits in general), "a tribe of
Indians living beyond the Pakaraima [mountains], who are men
by night, but fish by day," etc. (IT, 384), will doubtless remind
the reader strongly of the Huri Fish story (Sect. 152). People may
actually be transformed into fish (Sect. 115). The Piapocos of the
lower Guaviar, a branch of the Orinoco, have abelief in Evil Spirits
who live by day at the bottom of the water, but emerge at night,
when they walk about, screaming like little children: they caU these
Spirits Mami-naimis, and consider that the various rock-carvings are
their handiwork (Cr, 525, 529). Endowed with somewhat similar
habits there must be included here the Water People mentioned by
Brown (Bro, 247), who apparently received his information from the
Tarumas of the upper Essequibo, and by Cr^vaux (274) who derived his from the Indians of the upper Parou, in the far eastern
Guianas. The former tells us that the Toonahyannas, or Water
People, are said to hve more to the south, near the headwaters of the
Trombetas River (in Brazil). These have ponds encircled bystockades, to which they retire for the night, sleeping with their
bodies submerged. The latter authority states that "on a march of
four days to the westward, we would meet some very bad Indians
whom it would be impossible to take by surprise because they plunged
in a stream called by the same name (Parou) as that which we were
now on. . . . Let us note in passing that tooTia signifies 'water' not
only amongst the Taruma, but also in the language of the Trios,
Roucouyennes, Apalai, Carijonas: the Caribs of the Antilles call
water tone." Perhaps these Water People were imdergoiog a gradual
transformation before reaching the final change with advancing
European civilization, after the style of the Partamonas at Waipah
village on the Ireng, who stated that it was currently reported among
the surrounding inhabitants that now that a white man had come
among them, their country would sink under water (Bro, 283).

179. When zoomorphic the Water Spirit may take on the form of
a porpoise, manati (Sect. 183), macaw, snake, or fish. Thus, the
Pomeroon Arawaks believe in the kassi-kuyuha, a white or a black
variety of porpoise: the latter will hunt and injure a person who
happens to fall into the water, whereas the white species will save one
from drowning and carry him to shore. All that one has to do is
to jump on the Spirit's back — it will do the rest and will always help
anyone who is not afraid of it. Caroquia, on the Demerara River,
is a place avoided by the Indians: Water-m&mmas in this place
take the form of huge scarlet macaws, which rise out of the river
and drag them beneath the water, woodskins and all (Ki, 179). On
the Moruca River an old Warrau piai friend of mine told me that
it is the macaw who tells the Ho-ar&nni to come and upset the canoe,
as well as to destroy the occupants: the bird itself may also assist
directly in the work of destruction.

180. The Caribs talk of their Okoyumo being like a camudi snake,
but much bigger; it Uves in undergroimd water: in habitat, it
corresponds closely to the variety of Water Spirit which the Warraus
call Ahtiba. In cases of snake-bite among certain tribes, in addition
to any other treatment the bitten person must neither drink water,
bathe, nor come into the neighborhood of water, during the period
immediately following the accident [cf. Sect. 317]: the same prohibition, for a similar period, is incumbent on his children, his parents, and
his brothers and sisters so long as they reside in the same settlement.
His wife alone is free from the taboo (ScR, ii, 130). The freedom of
the woman from such an inconvenience is interesting when regarded in
conjunction with the belief in human milk as an eflBcacious antidote
for snake-poison.

244 ANIMISM AND FOLK-LOEE OF GUIANA INDIANS [eth. ANN. 30

181. Of Water Spirits in tlie form of fish I must note the Omars,
of which, so far as the name is concerned, the only record I can find
is given by im Thurn. These are beings —

With bodies variously described as like those of exaggerated crabs and fish, who
live under water in the rapids, and often drag down the boats of the Indians as they

shoot these places A story was told me at Ouropocari fall on the Essequibo. . . .

This Omar used to feed on rotten wood, and he dragged down many boats merely in
mistake for floating logs, but all the same the Indians were drowned. So one day an
Ackawoi peaiman carefully wrapped up two pieces of the wood with which fire is
rubbed, so that no water could make them damp. Then he dived down into the middle of the falls, and got into the belly of the Omar. There he found whole stores of
rotten wood. So he set fire to this. Then the Omar, in great pain, rose to the surface, belched out the peaiman and died. [IT, 385.J

I do not know whether this author was aware that omar is the
Arawak term for that terrible little fish, the pirai, whose peculiarly
destructive powers would constitute a capital groundwork on which
to weave fabulous embellishment, though there is a suspicion that
the word is but a play on the word Jonah, the exploits of these
extraordinary individuals being so closely parallel.

183. I obtained a somewhat similar story from the Warraus of the
Moruca River.

The Piai in the Water Spirit's Belly (W)"

generation he carried with him, in his corial, banab posts, firewood, and fire. Before
taking his departure he warned his wife that perhaps Ho-ar4nni would swallow him
also, but that if not, she might expect him to return within, a month. He traveled
down the stream, and turning a jwint, his boat was suddenly engulfed within the open
jaws of the Water Spirit there lying in wait: boat, posts, firewood, and fire were all
swallowed with him. When at last the piai "caught himself ' [i. e. came to his senses],
he was in complete darkness; so after lighting his fire, he began to make himself
comfortable and set up his banab, by sticking the half-dozen rods in. regular sequence
deep into the Water Spirit's belly. Ho-ardnni naturally experienced acute pain and
went to consult a piai friend of his who, however, could give him no relief, but advised
him to go elsewhere. The sufferer therefore visited another medicine-man, who told
him practically the same thing: "I cannot help you. It is just what you can expect
for treating people of my profession in the way you do. " As a last resource he went to
a third doctor, of even greater renown than the others, but by this time the piai
within was making the pains ten times worse, with the heaping up of the firewood
on the lighted fire, and the sticking in of the posts around. All the consolation he got

It was but the work of a minute to get her\ninto his boat, and she was indeed beautiful to look upon. So beautiful was she that\nhe carried her home to his mother, and made her his wife, the only condition that\nOriyu stipulated being that neither her prospective husband nor her mother-in-law\nshould ever divulge her origin. Being so accustomed to the water, Oriyu proved an\nexcellent helpmate: out she would go with her husband, in his boat, and look into\nthe depths for fish. These she could see when no one else could, and she would advise\nhim not to throw his line in here, but over there, and so on. And thus day after day\nthey returned home, always bringing the old mother-in-law plenty of fish. As you\ncan well imagine, this happiness did not last very long; it came to an end through\nthe old woman, when in liquor, loosening her tongue and letting out the secret of\nOriyu's origin. Oriyu said nothing at this time, so grieved she was, but she waited\nher opportunity to take her husband with her to her former home under the\nwaters. So on the next occasion that the crabs began to \"march\" from out the ocean\nto the shore, the family made up a large party, and all took their places, with their\nquakes, in a big corial. As they were coming down the river, Oriyu all of a sudden\ntold her companions that she and her husband were about to pay a visit to her people\nbelow, but that they would not be gone long, and that in the meantime she would send\nup something for them to eat and drink, but they must share everything fairly\nWithout more ado she and her man dived into the water. After awhile up came a\nlarge 'jar of cassiri, and a lot of potatoes, a very welcome addition to the few provisions they had on board. When they had each had their fill of the cassiri, and\nhad eaten the potatoes, they threw the jug and the useless skins back into the water,\nwhere the Oriyu turned the former into the giant low-low [Silurus] and the latter\ninto the squatty little imiri [Sciadeicthys]. This is why we old Arawaks always speak\nof the low-low as the fisherman's water-jug, and of the imiri as his potatoes.\n\n185. Brett mentions certain other good qualities of the Oriyus.\nOut on one of the islands all the men, women, and children were\nstruck down with sickness. ArawdniH [cf. Hariwah, Sect. 3], the\nisland chieftain, begged Oriyu for some charm to withstand the Evil\nSpirit's power which had made his people sick. She gave him the\nbranch of an Ida tree, which she told him to go and plant, and\nto bring back to her the first fruit that should fall from it. This\nturned out to be a calabash (Crescentia) , with which he did what he\nwas told. Having emptied the rind through certain holes cut in it,\nshe provided him with the feathered handle, and dived into the sea\nwhence she brought the shining white stones to put into it; with\nthese she thereupon showed him how to invoke the Spirits. Thus\nwas the first maraka (rattle) formed. Besides this, she taught\nArawaniM the use of tobacco, till then unknown to man (BrB, 18).\n\n186. Like the Spirits of the Forest, the Oriyus have strong sexual\npredilections. Every night, in their anthropomorphic form, both\nmales and females may come after Indians of the opposite sex,\nrespectively, and no disastrous result follows the intimacy.' But\nthe Indians who happen to have such dealings must keep the fact\nabsolutely secret: if divulged, either they will not live long, or they\n\n1 Among some of the old Warraus the product of an abortion is described as the Water Spirit's child\nbeing 2 or 3 inches long, with the head like that of a horse and the feet like those of a lizard.\n\nwill never be visited again by their Spirit friends. Furthermore,\nthose Indians who foster such friendships must on no account have\nsimilar dealings with their own people.' How THE Water Spmrr Got the Man's Wife from Him (W)"

She was very anxious to accompany him in the corial, but he insisted\non her remaining and of course she had to obey. Being very tired, she soon afterward\nfell asleep, and about midnight the Water Spirit paid her a visit. . . Halfdazed, she woke up, and asked him whether he had done anything to her, and when\nhe told her that he had, recognizing a stranger's voice in place of her husband's, she\nfelt very much ashamed. However, the Water Spirit told her who he was, of his\ngreat love for her, and that he would now take her to wife: all she had to do was to\ntell her previous husband that it was entirely his fault that she had been left alone\nand taken advantage of, and that henceforth she declined to share his hearth and\nhome. So when the latter returned next morning from his fishing, the wife made a\nclean breast of everything, for which she blamed him, as he had refused to let her\naccompany him in the corial, and she told him further that she intended living with\nhim no more. They started now on their way home, and getting into the boat, they\npaddled a short distance, when the wife said: \"After today you will not see me. You\nmust tell all my family to meet me tomorrow at a spot that I will show you.\" As\nthey traveled along, she showed him the very spot and at the same moment the boat\nstopped, just as if some one were holding it. She got out, the water coming up to her\nknees, and the corial continued on its journey. After a while the husband turned\naround to have a look, and saw his wife with another man, the Water Spirit, just stepping ashore: as he turned the point, the couple were walking together along the riverbank. Now, when he reached home without his wife, all her people wanted to know\nwhat had become of her; the mother especially was angry, but became somewhat\nmollified when he assured her that next day he would take her to the very place\nwhere her daughter had left him. He also gave her a message from his late wife that\nshe was to bring the silver nose-ornament and the bead bracelets and necklets which\nthe latter had left behind. So on the following morning he took the mother down to\nthe river-bank, and there sure enough they saw the guilty couple, the daughter and\nthe Water Spirit, behaving in a very friendly manner. As they got quite close, the\nSpirit suddenly disappeared, leaving the woman by herself. The mother then handed\nover the beads and ornaments, while her daughter murmured: \"Your son-in-law\ncaused this trouble: he would not let me come into the corial with him; and so when\nI was fast asleep the Water Spirit took advantage of me.\" Mother and daughter\nsobbed, and the latter said: \"You will see me sometimes, but never distinctly: directly\nyou think you see me clearly, I will disappear.\" No one knew at the time that the\nWater Spirit had taken advantage of the man also: but it was this Spirit who had\nmade the husband refuse to let his wife keep him company in the corial, so as the\nbetter to carry out his wicked design.\n\n1 This e^lains a curious phase of Indian character: Celibacy in either sex is regarded as something\nuncanny or unnatural. It is on this account tliat two very respected residents in my district, leading\npresumably irreproachable celibate lives, were believed by many of the Indians to have enjoyed intimate\nrelations with the Oiiyu.\n\n248 ANIMISM AND FOLK-LOEE OF GUIANA INDIANS [bth. This is exactly\nwhat did occur. When the man and his friends had filled their quakes and boarded\nthe corial , he told them that he had acted in an evil way to a girl among the crab bushes,\nand that when the boat suddenly stopped of its own accord, he would have to jump\nout, but that he would join them later on. After a while the corial suddenly came to\na standstill, oiu' friend jumped out, and his friends left him standing in the water\nwhere the girl was holding him up. They reached home at last, and on arrival at the\nlanding-place their women were waiting to carry the crabs up to the house. The one\nwho was disappointed at not seeing her husband asked what had become of Mm.\nThey told her that he had acted wrongly with a girl, and that they had left him behind.\nIn the meantime the erring spouse was taken by the Ho-ardnni girl [Sect. 777] to her\npeople below, and her father told him that he had been sent for because his daughter\nwanted him. But he added: \"You can go home to your own people this very day,\nand enjoy the feast of crabs that you and your friends have been gathering. I make\nonly this one condition. If there is any disturbance or fighting at the sport, you must\ncome back here at once: otherwise, you may remain with your own people, and we\nwill not trouble you further. I am sending both my daughters with you.\" And so\nit came to pass that the two girls took him to his own landing-place, and when they\ngot near, they told him to shut his eyes. As soon as he opened them again he found\nhimself on land, close to his house. He entered, and telling every one \"how day?\"\nsat down: his wife brought him food and drink. But as the evening progressed, the\npeople all began to be quarrelsome in their cups, with the result that his brothers-inlaw, sisters-in-law, and wife all threatened to beat him for sporting with the strange\ngirl. This was quite enough for him. He rushed out of the place right back to the\nlanding, where the two Water Women were awaiting him, and who asked why he\nwas not enjoying himself at the party. But when he told them how his people had\ncommenced to interfere, and had threatened to beat him, they took him back into\nthe water, where the old Ho-ar4nni father said, \"Take my two daughters to wife.\"\n\n188. These Water People have great Hkiiig for women at the\nmenstrual period, so much so that, at such a time, no Carib, Akawai,\nWarrau, or Arawak woman will travel by boat or even cross water.\n\nThe Moon-sick Girl and the Water Spirit (C)\n\nA young girl had reached the age when she was developing certain signs indicative of\napproaching womanhood. When he had sat on it some\ntime the old man said, \"I sent you my daughter for your wife: you must live a good\nUfe, and must now send down your sister for my son. \" This was all agreed to, and the\nman's Ho-ar4imi wife brought him dry boiled meat and cassava: the eating done,\nshe gave hijn to drink. Not only are many of tlie troubles aflBicting mankind, as just\nrecorded in the legend, ascribable to the machinations of Oriyu, but\nhe (or she) is held responsible for more than one natural phenomenon.\nThe tidal wave, or bore, known as appapuru [an Arawak term] on the\nB^bice and other streams, in certain of this colony's rivers is a case\nin point. Among the natives the popular explanation is that when\nthis River becomes inconveniently low for the had things of the deep,\nthey show their uneasiness by moving furioiisly about, and thus\nagitate the river (Da, 21). The several tribes on the coast, we learn\nfrom Doctor Hancock, usually give it some name, signifying \"head\nof waters\" or \"mother of waters,\" and in connection with this have\nmany strange stories to tell of the Loku-kuyuha (people's spirit) mermaid, or \"watery mamma\" as they translate it (ScC, 288). Again,\nWailak-paru, a creek on the right bank of the Potaro, is so called\nfrom a part of the himian body, and is beheved to be the home of\nOriyu: the tm-bulence of the water as it nms into the Potaro is\ncaused by water issuing from the body of that Spirit.\n\n192. The Water Spirits must not be talked about, nor may their\nnames be mentioned.\n\nAmaxxa and her T.^lkative Husband (C)\n\nHeated with the fumes and liquor of a big paiwarri feast, an Indian succeeded in\nmaking his way to the pond where he intended bathing his skin and getting cool.\nOn arrival there, he was met by Amanna, one of the Okoyumo Nation, a very pleasantspoken woman, who asked him to join her in the water. He demurred at first, but\nwhat with her repeated requests coupled with the attractiveness of her physical\ncharms, he ultimately consented. Even at the last moment, he said he felt sure that\nhe would be drowned ; but she promised to look after him and see that no harm befell.\nWhen they got below the surface, he saw a number of houses, plentj- of people, and\nmany young women: he felt quite content now, especially when the latter offered\nhim drink. But Amanna would have none of this, and took him straight away to her\nold father, vho gave him welcome and instructed his daughter to look after him\nproperly. And tliis she did. In the meantime the man's mother had missed hiTn\nfrom the convivial gathering, and following his tracks, traced them to the water's edge;\nand there the tracks disappeared. '\"My poor son must have been drowned,\" she murmured, and proceeded to look for his floating body; but of course it was nowhere to be\nseen, and she mourned him a long time as dead. Thus, time slipped on, and the desire\ncame on him to see his mother; so he \\'isited her. After she had asked him where he had\n\n252 ANIMISM AND FOLK-LOBE OF GUIANA INDIANS [eth. ann. 30\n\nbeen in the meanwhile, he told her that he had been for a \"walk-about.\" This made\nthe old woman say: \"Well, you must not go away again, because I am aged now and\nstarving. I cannot depend on your little brother to support me, and you know I have\nno other children.\" But the man had a bad mind, and went back that very afternoon\nto his Water Spirit wife, and on this occasion remained with her even longer than he\nhad done before. When at last he returned after his second absence, he found his,\nmother and little brother drinking paiwarri. The latter questioned him point blank\nas to whether he was living with the Okoyumo People. This naturally made him\nextremely angry and, with a \"How dare you ask me such a question?\" he hurried\nback to the water, where he remained a still longer period than that of his second\nabsence. In the meantime Amanna had borne him three children, and leaving the\nlatter behind, he told his wife to accompany him on a visit to his mother. The couple\non arrival found the old mother and her younger son again at a drinking party, but\nthis time the son was absolutely drunk, and nothing would do but he must ask his\nelder brother as before whether he was living with the Okoyumo People. \"Yes,\nI am ! \" replied the exasperated man, ' ' and this is my wife, Amanna, one of that nation . ' '\nDirectly the woman heard this, she made all haste to the waterside, and jumped into\nthe water, her husband in close pursuit. As soon as he got below her friends and relatives set on him and killed him for having mentioned her name and telling people\nwho she was.\n\n193. Besides their dislike to hearing mention of their names and\nantecedents, as well as their passion for menstruating women, it is\ninteresting to note the strong objection of the Water Spirits to a\npot-spoon being washed outside of the traveling boat in either river\nor sea (Sects. 214, ^19)."

The surest way of offending the Water Spirits, however, and\nthereby getting caught in a storm, and being capsized, wrecked, or\ndi'owned by way of punishment, is to utter certain words strictly\nforbidden under the circumstances. The same holds good for Cayenne, where the superstitious\nIndians take care not to speak of several things by their right names :\n\nthus, if one has to speak of a rock, it must be described as \" that which\nis hard;\" if it is a Hzard, they must similarly paraphrase by saying\n\"that which has a long tail.\" It is dangerous also to name the\nstreams and little islands that they pass en route. But\nshe chased him. The girl wanted him very much, and as she got close to the spot\nwhere he waa, whispered, \"Don't you want me?\" Instead of replying quietly, however, Waiamari loudly upbraided her by shouting BiUU Kwahorol [\"Incest 1 Shajne ! \"),\nand the girl drew back. At any rate the couple got out of the\nwater, and came up to the house, which the aimt entered, the boy passing on to go\nto stay with his elder uncle, Okohi, at whose place he slept that night. Now, the\nvery fact of not going home as usual with his aunt made Waiamari guilty in the eyes\nof her husband, who followed his nephew next morning to Okohi's place. When he\nreached there, he reproached his nephew for having attempted improper conduct\nwith his wife, a charge which was indignantly denied. At any rate, they started\nfighting and the uncle was thrown down. They fought again and the imcle was\nthrown a second time. Okohi now interfered, and said, \"Boy! That will do,\" and\nso stopped the contention between his brother and nephew. Wau-u! 199. A peculiar custom among the Makusis, practised as soon as the
new moon is visible (Sect. 227), is that of all the men standing before
the doors of their huts, and drawing their arms backward and forward
in its direction at short intervals : by this means they are strengthened
for the chase (ScR, n, 328). "As soon as the new moon appears, they
aU run out of their huts and cry Loole at ths moon! . . . They take
certain leaves, and after rolling them in the shape of a small funnel,
they pass some drops of water through it into the eye, while looking
at the moon. This is very good for the sight" (BBR, 228). The
first night of the incoming moon was considered the proper occasion
for obtaining clay for the manufacture of pots and other utensils
which, it was beUeved, would not speedily be broken (Sect. £58).

200. With regard to the explanations given as to the nature of the
ecUpse of the moon, I have obtained the following at firstr-hand from
the Pomeroon Arawaks. The phenomenon is due to its traveUng
along the Sun's path, faUing asleep, and so not being able to get out
of the way quickly enough. With the object of awakening the Moon
members of this tribe strike drums, blow shells, and make a big noise
generally, whenever the echpse takes place. They must also keep
themselves lively and active, and during the whole night must eat
absolutely nothing; were they to break the fast, they would change
into whatever animal or plant they might be eating (Sect. £4^).
Indeed, it is a common beUef among these people that, at the time of
an echpse, there is a constant change or transformation-scene taking
place on Nature's stage, in both animal and vegetable kingdoms,
owing to tliis cause. The transformation is not necessarily sudden
but may take time. I can call to mind an old Arawak story of a hunt«r
who had gone to visit one of the streams away back from the Monica
River: On the first occasion he sees a huge land-camudi; on the
second, at the time of an ecUpse, he finds the snake changed into a
tapir; and on the third he sees it swimming in the water as a manati.

201. As to the Orinoco Indian tribes, GumiUa has left us some very
interesting records concerning the eclipse of the moon. Some of
these nations beheved that it was about to die: others that it was
angry with them, and that it would give them no more light. The
LoMca and Atabdca Indians held to the death theory (G, 11, 274)
and were under the conviction that if the Moon were indeed to die,
all exposed fires would be extinguished. Their women, crying and
yelUng — an outburst in which the men joined — accordingly would
each seize a glowing ember and hide it, either in the sand or underground. Moved by their tears and entreaties, the Moon however
recovers, and the hidden fires are extinguished: but were he indeed
to 'die, the concealed embers would remain ahght. The Sahvas had
different views (G, 11, 277). All the warriors stand up in rows facing
the Moon, offering liim their prowess and strength and entreating

15961°— 30 ETH— 15 17

258 ANIMISM AND FOLK-LOBE OF GUIANA INDIANS [bth. ann. 30

him not to leave them. The young nien, of 15 to 20 years of age,
stand in two rows apart while certain old men roughly thrash them
in turn with whips. Finally, the women, in a sea of tears bewail
the Moon's projected departure and fatal absence. The idea would
seem to be that the Moon has enemies whom, through fear, he is
anxious to avoid, and he is therefore desirous of giving the benefit
of his light to other nations. It is only the promises of these Indian
warriors to fight in his favor which allay his fears, and hence there is
no necessity for him really to take himself off. As soon as the
Guay^nas (G, ii, 278) recognize an eclipse of the moon, they take up
the implements used in cultivating their fields. With much talk
and gesticulation, some cut the undergrowth, others clear it, and
others again dig up the ground, all of them loudly proclaiming that the
Moon has cause for being annoyed, and particularly good reason for
forsaking them, considering that they had never made a field for him.
They accordingly beg him not to go, because they are now providing
him with a field, in which they propose planting maize, cassava, and
plantains. With these promises and entreaties they continue at
their task, working on it with vigor so long as the eclipse lasts; and,
as soon as it is over, they return to their houses overjoyed. But
there is no more working on the field in the Moon's behalf until the
next eclipse takes place! Among the Otomacs (G, ii, 279), when the
event occurs, the husbands aimlessly take up their weapons, skip
about, and yell beyond measure, stretch the arrow on the bow in
sign of anger, and ask, beg, and implore the Moon not to die. While
they continue in their grief, the Moon goes on diminishing and languishing. Kecoghizing from this that their actions are not understood, they run back to their houses, where they bitterly reproach
their wives for not grieving over and bewailing the Moon's sickness.
The latter make not the slightest sign that they understand what is
expected of them, and answer never a word. The men then change
their tactics and start begging and beseeching their wives to cry
and weep, so that the Moon may revive and not die. Still the
women act as if they do not understand what is besought of them.
So the men give them presents — glass-beads, monkey-tooth necklaces, jewelry, and the like. The women now understand in truth,
and saying many prayers soon make the Moon shine as bright and
clear as before — for doing which they earn their husbands' gratitude.
According to their idea it is the female voices that move the Moon
to take compassion on them, and save them from extinction."

eclipse, Jurupari (Sect. 101) is killing the Moon; they make all the
noise they can to frighten him away (ARW, 348). So again, the
Island Caribs say that Maboya (Sect. 84) is eating the Moon on such
an occasion: they dance all night, and rattle their calabashes with

little pebbles inside (RoP, 461). Schomburgk points out the curious
fact that the Taruma word for a moon eclipse is fiwa-toto, the hteral
translation of which is 'Moon-Earth' (ScR, ii, 469).

203. Any reference to comets in the Indian literatme is extremely
scarce. With regard to the one that was seen by Schombiu-gk in the
early forties, the Arekunas and Makusis regarded it as a sign of
pestilence, famine, and disaster. One night they all emerged from
their huts . . . men, women, and children extended their arms expressive of supplication and beseeched it to leave the heavens, so that
they should not come to grief under its influence . . . the Makusis
called it Ca-po-eseLma, " Fire-Cloud," or Wae-inopsa, " Sun that throws
its rays behind"; the Arekunas gave it the name of Wa-taima, and
the Wapisianas Capische, both terms signifying "Spirit of the Stars"
(ScR, II, 308). The Pomeroon Arawaks speak of the present year's
(1910), Halley's, comet, simply as Wiwa-kihi-koro Git. "Star-tailwith"), but have no information to furnish concerning it. Among
the Island Caribs, Limacani is a comet sent by Coualina, the "boss" of
the Chemeens [i. e., Familiar Spirits] to cause evil when he is vexed
(BBR, 231).

303A. In the Makusi legend of Murapa-yeng (lit. Bat Mountain,
one of the Pakaraima Range) the phenomenon is ascribed to an old
woman carrying a fire-stick under somewhat pathetic circumstances:
Schomburgk tells the story.

The Legend of Bat Mountain

A long, long while ago, an immense Bat Uved on the mountain and spread fear and
terror among the Makusis. As soon as the Sun had sunk in the west, the huge creature
left its unknown dwelling, swept down upon the happy homes, and, swift as an arrow,
pounced upon and carried off anyone whom it found out of doors: it carried the individual in its powerful claws up to its unknown nest and there devoured him. Fear
reigned of an evening throughout the settlements and in the huts, and lamentation
filled the air of a morning when often two, sometimes three, persons would be missing;
not a night passed without an abduction, the tribe daily numbered less, and its entire
annihilation seemed at hand. The medicine-man exorcised the Spirit; it returned
again: the men went to discover the residence of the ciirsed murderer, but they did
not find it — ^Makunaima was not with them. To prevent the total destruction of her
tribe an old woman arose and declared herself ready to sacrifice herself for the good
of her nation. When night fell, she stationed herself, with a covered fire-stick, in
the middle of the village while the remainder of the people crouched in terror within
their houses. The fluttering of the wings is heard, and the heroine, seized in the
creature's frightful claws, is carried aloft to the chamel house. She now uncovers
the fire-stick, which like the Sun throwing its rays backward (the Cometh, shows by
the streak of light thus produced the direction that the people must foUow to find
the mortuary house of their brethren. The high flames of fire from the burning nest
upon this very mdUntain showed the folk next morning where to go : they succeeded in
kiUing the creatiire. History does not say whether the old woman lost her life in this
heroic deed; but even now immense heaps of bleached bones are to be found there.

204. Axawalffi, Warraus, in fact all the Indian tribes of whom we
have reliable accounts, possess myths and legends indicative of a
more or less animistic conception of the stars and constellations.

Dance (270) says that Eweiwah, or Huewah (Arawak), and
Koiunuk (Akawai) are the names of the Morning and Evening stars
interchangeably, these tribes supposing that they are one and the same.
Brett (Br, 107), on the other hand, gives the Arawak name for Venus
as Warakoma [Waruk6ma], and that generally used for Jupiter as
Wiwa Kalimero (i. e. the star of brightness). The Warraus here on
the Pomeroon caU the Morning Star Okona-kura. She it was who
stuck in the hole when her people first came down from above the
skies to populate the earth (Sect. 51). The Makusis speak of the
Evening Star as Kai-wono, wife of the Moon, because she is to be
seen in his near neighborhood, and also on account of her shining
more brightly than all the other stars (ScR, n, 328). According to
Father Gili, the Indians of the Casiquiare believed that the dew
which falls by night was the spittle of the stars (AR, 207), a belief
similar to that reported of the Makusis. The Caribs ascribed it to the
urination of the stars (ScR, i, 429). The Makusis speak of shooting
stars as Wai-taima (ScR, ii, 328). The Island Caribs regarded all the
heavenly bodies as Carib. Father de la Borde mentions some j&ve
or six stars in their cosmogony, but unfortunately has apparently
not identified them. Racumon was one of the first Caribs made by
Louquo ; he was transformed into a large snake with the head of a
man; he was always seated on a cabatas (a hard and high tree);
he lived on its fruit, which resembles a large plum or small apple,
and which he gave sometimes to those who passed; he is now changed
into a star. " Savacou was also a Carib. He was changed into a
large bird; he is the captain of the Storms and Thunders; he has
caused the heavy rains, and is also a star now. Achinaon, a Carib,
at present a star, causes light rain and strong winds. Couroumon
(a Carib), also a star, causes the heavy sea waves, and upsets canoes;
he is also the cause of flood and ebb." (BBR, 229.)"
}

  "passage_text": "305. Arawaks speak of the MUky Way under two names, one of\nwhich signifies the Path of the Maipuri (Tapir), and the other is the\nPath of the Bearers of Wai-6, a species of white clay of which their\nvessels are made. The nebulous spots are supposed to be the tracks\nof Spirits whose feet were smeared with that material (Br, 107).\nOn equally reliable authority we are told that the three nebulsB\nwithin the Milky Way represent a tapir being chased by a dog, followed by a jaguar, who is not particular in choice, so that he take\neither the dog or the tapir. Another legend is that the nebulse were\nformed by celestial wUd hogs rooting up the white clay (Da, 296).\nThe Makusis call the Milky Way Parana, a term which they apply also\nto the sea.\n\n306. With regard to the Southern Cross, Dance talks of it as being\nthe great White Crane, and gives a legend relative to it (Da, 296).\nArawaks and Warraus, however, have told me that this represents the\npowis {Crax sp.), the nearer \"pointer\" to it being the Indian just\nabout to let fly his arrow, the farther one indicating his companion\nwith a fire-stick running up behind. This constellation serves also\nas an indication for the hunting of the bird, Schomburgk recording\n(ScT, 23) how, when the Cross stands erect, the powis commences\nits low moan (Sect. 98). The Makusis apparently regard the Southern\nCross as the home of the Spirit of this bird.\n\n207. There are two groups of stars described by the Arawaks and\ncertain of the Warraus, as the Babracote and the Camudi: four bright\nstars (Pegasus) with four imaginary connecting lines constitute the\nsquare frame of the former, another thick cluster (Scorpio) representing the Snake. This is' the Arawak story:\n\nThe Babeacote and Camudi (A)\n\nThere was a man living with, his wife and mother-in-law in the same house: the\nwife's father had been dead a long time. The mail was always going out hunting, but,\nalthough he started early, and returned late, luck never seemed to attend his efforts.\nThis made the mother-in-law very angry, and one day she said to him: \"You are a\nworthless son-in-law. Day after day, you go out hunting, and you bring back nothing.\nDay after day, you go out fishing, and bring back nothing.\" The man made no reply\nto all this, but just laid himself quietly down in his hammock where he remained\nuntil next morning. Next morning he called his wife and told her to pack the hammocks with sufficient cassava for two or three days, as he intended taking her out\nhunting with him. After they had traveled a long way, he killed her, cut her into\npieces, and dried the flesh on a babracote. Next day he returned home with hin\nvictim's liver, and handing it to his mother-in-law said. \"Here's the Uver of a tapir\nfor you. The wife is laden with the flesh and is slowly coming on behind.\" The\nold woman, who was so hungry, spared no time in eating it, and when finished got\ninto her hammock quite satisfied, anxiously looking down the pathway for her daughter. After watching for some hours in vain, she began to think that the alleged tapir's\nliver must really have been her daughter's. Turning to her son-in-law, she charged\nhim with having killed her daughter, because it was then very late and still she had\nnot returned. He denied it and swore that she would soon be coming, but the woman\nwould not believe him. She continued watching until late in the night, and then\nshe knew that the Uver she had eaten was indeed her own daughter's. Of course\nshe slept but little, and early next morning crept quietly out of the house, and made\nher way to her brother, the large camudi, that lived at the head of the neighboring\ncreek. She told him how her son-in-law had killed her child, and given her the liver\nto eat. She told him also that she would send the culprit along that very creek, and\nthat as soon as he got within reach he was to catch and swallow him. When she reached\nhome again the old woman said nothing, but next day told her son-in-law that she\nwas feeling very hungry, that he must go out hunting, and that if he went up to the\nhead of the creek, he would find plenty of game to shoot. The son-in-law suspected\nBomething, so he went to a younger brother of his and told him to put in a day's hunting at the head of that very same creek, while he took good care to take his bow and\narrows in exactly the opposite direction. That same evening, instead of returning\nto his own place, he came back to his younger brother's house. No brother returned\n\n262 ANIMISM AND FOLK-LOBE OF GTHANA INDIANS [eth.ann.30\n\nthat night, nor the next day. Indeed, he never came back, because he had been\nkilled and swallowed by the camudi, who had mistaken his man. The son-in-law,\nafter waiting theie a few days, then knew what had happened, and niade his way\nto another settlement, far, far from the nagging old woman. On a clear night you\ncan still see the babracote where he barbecued his wife, and close to its side you can\njust make out the camudi with its swollen belly, due to the younger brother being\ninside."

The Pleiades, the Seven Stars, bore a very important r61e in\nthe daily life of the Guiana Indians in that, among several other\nreasons, their rising from the east marked the commencement of their\nnew year: this measm:ement of time was adopted from the Orinoco to\nCayenne. AH the legends relating to the constellations Taurus and\nOrion have something in common in the detail of an amputated arm\nor leg. Dance speaks of the Stars forming the belt and sword-sheath\nof the constellation Orion (Da, 343) as Mabukuli (Arawak) or Ibbehpughn (Akawai). Now the word Mabukuli signifies \"without leg,\"\nand the corresponding little story which he relates (Da, 296) will not\nprove out of place here : \" A huntsman being imsuccessful in the chase\none day, and being loth to return without flesh for his stepmother,\nwhom he loved, cut off one of his own legs, and wrapping it up in\nleaves, presented it to her as veritable game; and then ascended into\nthe heavens as Mabukuli (Ibbeh-pughn) or one-legged.\"\n\n309. The Legend of the Tumong, or Seven Stars, as told by Dance\n(296), apparently from Akawai sources, is this :\n\nThe Legend of the Seven Stars\n\nA man having lustful inclination toward bis brother's wife killed his brother while\nhunting in his company, and cutting off an arm of the murdered man, presented\nit to the widow as a proof of her husband's death. He then took her as his own wife.\nBut the spirit of the murdered man haunted a tree near by his brother's house, and\nfilled the air at nights with his laments, so that tHe widow, discovering the treachery\nof her new husband, became disconsolate. The fratricide, from vexation, decided to\nrid himself of her, and of her little child. For this purpose he took her ostensibly to\nhunt with him, and observing a hole at the root of a large tree, he desired her to stoop\nand search therein for a suspected acouri. While she looked in, he pushed her in completely, and also her child after her, and then stopped up the hole. On that idght\nthe spirit of the murdered man appeared to his brother and informed him that he\nknew of his deed of violence, and was not angry; for his wife had been transformed\ninto an acouri, and his child to an adourie, so that his unnatural malice, save by the\ninfliction of death, could not any more affect them. For himself, he would not cease\nto render the murderer's life miserable so long as his own mangled body remained\nunburied. But if the wicked brotlier would disembowel the body and scatter\nthe entrails, after interring the other remains, not only would the dead cease to be a\nterror, but at that season every year an abundance of fish would gather in the\nriver. The wretched brother then went to the place of the bloody deed, and did\nwhat he was told, when the scattered entrails of the murdered man floated upward\nto the skies, and assumed tlie appearance of the Seven Stars. And truly, as was\npredicted, on the annual appearance of those stars, the yarumak [Pimelodus maculatus], tibicurie [Prochilodus rubro-teniatus], caburessi [Chialceus tseniatus] and several\nother excellent fishes are abundant in the rivers.\n\nboth] the spibits of the sky. 263\n\n210. Every day Nohi-abassi went\nfarther and farther afield in the pursuit of game, and at length he reached a creek,\nwhere he climbed a tree, watching for the animals to come and quench their thirst.\nWhile waiting among the branches, he saw a woman wading up the creek toward\nthe tree and noticed that every time she put her hand into tne water she drew out\ntwo fish: one of these fish she put into her mouth; the other she put into her\nbasket. She was a very big woman, Nahakoboni by name.^ She was carrying a\ncalabash upside down, like a cap, upon her head, and would every now and again\ntoss it into the water; as she jerked it in, she made it swirl round and round like a\ntop, and there she would stand a few minutes watching it spinning on the surface.\nThen she would proceed on her way, put her hand into the water, draw out two fish\nagain, devour one, and place the other in her quake. And so she proceeded on her\nway, passed the tree where Nohi-abassi was in hiding, and still catching two fish at\na time, went on her way to the creek-head. Night caught the hunter, and so he\nhad to sleep up the tree. Next morning he reached home, and told his brother what\nhe had seen. . The latter said, \"I should like to see such a woman, who can catch so\nmany fish, and can eat them as well.\" But Nohi-abassi answered him: \"No! I\ndon't care to take you with me to show her to you: you are always laughing at everything, and you might laugh at her.\" And it was only when his brother faithfully\npromised not to laugh at anything that he might show him, that Nohi-abasai agreed\nto take him. So they started on their journey and reached the creek where\nthe adventure with the big woman had taken place the day before. Nohi-aba^\nclimbed the identical tree whence he had originally seen Nahakoboni, this tree being\nsituated a few yards away from the creek bank. His brother, however, who wanted to\nget a good look at the wonderful woman, insisted upon climbing a tree close to the\nwater's edge, and made his way up and along a branch which overhimg the stream.\nBoth brothers sat quiet, and by and by Nahakoboni came along as before, doing\njust the same thing, spinning her calabash, putting her hand into the water, drawing\nout two fish at a time, one of which she put into her mouth, the other into her basket.\nAt length she came along right underneath where the younger brother was in hiding,\nand recognized his shadow in the water. This shadow she tried again and again to\ncatch; she put her hand in quickly, first this side and then that, but of course she\ndid not succeed, and what with all her queer gesticulations and funny capers\nmade so ridiculous an appearance that the brother up above could not resist\nlaughing at her vain attempts to seize the substance for the shadow. He laughed\nagain and again and coiUd not stop laughing. Unfortimately for him, Nahakoboni,\nhearing the sound and looking up, recognized not onlyhimwhowas just over her head,\nbut also Nohi-abased, who was on the other tree some few yards distant. He said hib name was Wailya, that he liked her, and for the\nsame reason had assimied that form so as to have the chance of coming near her. He\ncame the next day, and the next, and every day while Wawaiya was on her way to\nthe field, and she became fonder and fonder of him. He finally tempted her, and\npromised her that if she followed him to the eastward, until earth and sky met, he\nwould resume his human shape and take her to wife. But she refused. So he\ncharmed her ax, and assured her that if she did what he told her to do, she would be\nsafe with him. Soon after, Serikoai asked Wawaiya to come with him and gather\navocado pears [Persea gratiisima], which were now ripe, so that while he climbed\nthe trees, she might collect firewood. She did so, and while her husband was up a\ntree, she went to grind her ax, but ever)- time it touched the stone it railed out, \"I\nmust cut. I must wound!\" [Sahtai!]. She asked her husband whether he could\nhear it talking, and he said , ' ' Yes ;' ' that it always spoke like that when being sharpened\nthere, but she must not worry over it. However, while Serikoai was descending\nthe tree she cut his leg clear through and took to flight. Though exhausted by loss\nof blood, Serikoai plucked an eyelash, and blew it into the air, where it became a\nbeautiful little bird, which he told to fly away to his mother's place and call his\nname. When the latter heard her son's name, she did not know what the bird meant,\nand so sent the bird back again to find out. On its return, she immediately rushed\noff and nursed her son so tenderly that he recovered of his wound. Serikoai now\nmanaged to walk about with a crutch, and took up the search to find his wife, but\nall traces of Wawaiya had then disappeared, what with the lapse of tune and the\nheavy rains. Nothing daunted, however, he traveled on and on, until at last he\ndiscovered a sprout of avocado pear. A little farther on he saw another, which\nre^ived his hope of finding her, because he now knew that she who had taken the\npears must have eaten them on the road, and cast the seeds by the wayside. Traveling\non and on, always to the eastward, he saw at last Wawaiya's and Wailya's footprints,\nand a little farther on saw them conversing right ahead of him. He thereupon shot\ntlie Tapir and, cutting off its head, implored his wife to return, saj-ing that if she\nrefused he would follow her fore\\er. She did refuse, however, and hurried on with\nher lover's spirit still after her, and her husband behind them both. Still rushing\nheadlong, the husband reached the earth's steep edge, where Wawaiya threw herself\ninto the deep blue skj-. If you watch on a clear night, you can still see Wawaiya\n\n266 ANIMISM AND FOLK-LOBE OF GUIANA INDIANS [bth. ann. 30\n\n[the Pleiades] with the Tapir's head [the Hyades: the red eye is Aldebaran] close\nbehind, and Serikoai [Orion, -with Rigel indicating the upper part of the sound limb]\nfarther back— all three in pursuit.\n\n311A.   "passage_text": "The Indians have the greatest superstition with regard to this bird, and would not\nkill it for any price. They say it keeps communication with the dead, and brings\nmessages to their conjurers. Even the common people on the coast retain in a great\nmeasure this superstition, and hold the bird in great awe. Its nocturnal habits, the\nswiftness and peculiarity of its flight, and its note, which breaks the silence of the\nnight, have no doubt contributed to the fear which Indians and Creoles entertain\nfor the'Wacarai or Sumpy Bird [ScT, 67].\n\nAs is the case with even far more civilized nations, owls are of\nequally evil portent and may indicate sickness, death,* the presence of\nan as-yet-unborn babe, or a birth. Thus, among the Pomeroon and\nMoruca Arawaks, the boku-boku, and the waro-baiya or maletitoro\n(both of them species of night-owl), and among the Demerara River\nArawaks, the hututu (night-owl) and makudi (small owl) are said\nalways to be heard when a person is sick or about to die. In the\nPomeroon the morokodyi (night-owl) cries when a female in the\nhouse is enciente. On the Demerara, when the night-owl calls\ncuta! cuta! cuta! quickly, it is to notify that one in the family is about\nto give birth to a child; and when that bird mews like a cat, it is the\nnotification of death (Da, 269). In French Guiana, on the upper\nParou River, at an Apalai village, Cr6vaux had a curious experience:\n\"Arrived in the forest where we proposed camping, we heard the notes\nof a bird which I have reason to believe is a kind of screech-owl. A\npanic seized my escort, the torches were put out, and men and women\nsaved themselves in the obscurity of the night. We were obUged to\nreturn to the village for our night's rest\" (Cr,300). OnthePomeroon\n\nand elsewhere, probably from their ciistom, when in lai^e numbers,\nof flying in pairs, one behind the other, the baridi hawks are taken\nas an omen of a fimeral. On the lower Amazon, a black eagle\n{MUvago nvdicoUis) locally known as the carac&ra-i, is considered a\nbird of Ul-omen by the Indians; it often perches on the tops of trees in\nthe neighborhood of their huts and is then said to bring a warning\nof death to some member of the household. Some say that its whining cry is intended to attract defenceless birds within its reach\n(HWB, 146). With regard to remaining species of birds, the Pomeroon Arawaks beheve that if the koko-bero flies over the house, some\none in it will shortly prove pregnant, that or a Uttle baby is about to\nbe taken sick. The voice of the kwar-kwarra brings an evil message,\nsimilar to that of the boku-boku. The kar6o-obannahu is a small\nnight-bird, so named after its note, Icarau! Jcarau! and obanndhu (the\nliver, the color of which it resembles). If its note is heard but\nfaintly, some individual must be exceedingly ill: if distinctly, the\npatient is getting better and stronger. When the beletika cries, some\none is about to be married; hence this token may be both of good\nand bad omen. Another set of bird-tokens may indicate approaching\nrainfall as well as accident (Sect. £17). There is still another class of\nomens, indicative of either prospective good luck or bad luck. Thus,\nwhen on a hunting expedition, one hears the karrasuri, a small bird,\nuttering a kind of laugh, he is sure to kill something, but if it should\ncry shirai, he will get nothing. According as the bukulaura, another\nbird, turns its back or its breast toward a person, so will fortune or\nmisfortune attend that person's wishes in obtaining whatever food\nhe wants. [Furthermore, when walking along the pathway one must\nnot mind if a munirikuti (species of black ant) bites his foot, because\nthis means that he will obtain something very good and satisfying.]\nSome Indians will never turn their back on a trogon : \" He [the Indian]\nattributed his safety (from drowning) to the strictness with which the\nIndians had observed the proper respect due to a trogon that had\nflown over our heads in the morning: they have a superstition that\nif, on setting out on a journey, they should turn their backs to this\nspecies of bird, ill luck will surely foUow.\" (BW, 146: on the Mazaruni, with an Arawak and Akawai crew.) The following are some\nmiscellaneous examples of bird-omens: On the Pomeroon one must\nnot gaze too long on the great red macaw, imless the individual wishes\nto become bald, presumably in view of the bird having its cheeks so\nmarkedly devoid of feathers. The advent of strangers is notified by\nthe warracabba (trimipeter-bird) when it is seen playing about near\nthe house, having in its mouth a leaf with which it is beheved to be\nbuilding a banab. On the Orinoco, in token of the Father coming\nto visit them, the Cacique said that on the previous day he had seen a\nbird with pecuhar feathers and colors passing over his house: it gave\n\n276 ANIMISM AND ^OLK-LOfiE OF GUIANA INDIANS [bth.ann.SO\n\nthem notice of his approach (G, i, 311). Children are discouraged\nfrom picking up certain feathers, as these tend to weaken memory,\nand the handling of the feathers of a scissor-tail hawk, called by the\nAtorais chaouneh, conduces to insanity (Da, 250).\n\n3;33A. The trio played the same trick at many a\nsettlement, until one day the owl t«Id them he had to travel about for a while, and\nthat during his absence they must behave themselves, and stay indoors at night, as\notherwise trouble would be sure to happen. But no sooner had Boku-boku turned\nhis back, than the bats, imable to resist temptation, continued their evil courses.\nThey got to a place one night where the fish were being dried, but having no owl with\nthem on this occasion, they could not shout hohvJ bohvJ bohu! as loudly as they\ndid before; hence, the people not being so frightened now, ran away only a little\ndistance, just far enough to be able to watch everything and to see that it was only the\nbats who were stealing their food. But the bats, remaining undisturbed, thought\nthey could now do what they liked with impunity, and hence returned again upon\nthe following evening, when the people remained just as they were, some seated,\nsome lying in their hammocks. The bats still thought of course tliat nothing bad\ncould happen them, and were laughing (MI chi! chi! for very joy. But the housemaster took out his bow aad arrow, the latter tipped with a knob of wax, with which\nhe shot one of them on the rump, stunning it.^ The other bat, escaping into the\nforest, met Boku-boku, who had just returned from his travels, and to whom he narrated the circmnstances of his brother's untimely death. Nothing daunted, the two\nreturned to hunt that night, and on this occasion the noise of their voices, now that it\nincluded the owl's, created such a stir that the folk ran as before into the bush, while\nBoku-boku and his brother-in-law stole the fish. But lying on the babracote was\nthe dead bat, which they took home with them, and there they soundly smacked\nhim on the spot where he had been struck with the arrow: this brought him round, the\nfire not having withered him up beyond recovery, and he laughed chi/ chi/ chi! on\nawakening. And although Boku-boku was prevented accompanying them the\nfollowing evening, the two bats insisted on repeating their nocturnal excursion: as\nbefore, the folk were not frightened, and again one of the bats got shot in his posterior.\nNext night, the surviving bat returned with Boku-boku, and they found as before upon,\nthe babracote, the body of their relative: this they took away with them, but on this\noccasion, when they smacked the corpse, it never woke — ^it had been dried too much\nover the fire. The surviving bat however continues to take his revenge u pon people\nand sucks them and their fowls, as well as doing other damage, while the presence of\nBoku-boku, his brother-in-law, invariably means mischief: when heard at night,\nsome one is surely about to sicken and die.\n\n334. There are two bees which indicate the arrival of a stranger.\nOne of these insects (honorari) comes in the morning early, and in\nthe afternoon late, while the other (wariro) Uves in the ground;\nwhen either of these buzzes Arawaks are convinced that people are\nabout to visit them. The modudu is another bee that flies round\n\nI On the upper Aiary the children's toy arrows are tipped with a button of black wax (KG, i, 106-7).\n\nsomewhere between 4 and 5 a. m.: should a young person hear it\nbuzzing he (or she) must immediately get out of the hammock, on\npenalty of having pains all over the body. The Arawaks of the\nPomeroon believe that if a candle-fly, Pyrophorus noclilucus (koko-i)\nis seen coming into the house, it may mean three things: supposing\nit falls to the ground, this indicates the near death of one of the\ninmates; if it falls into the fire, this shows that a deer has sent it\nalong to fetch a light for him; but if it settles down under the roof,\nthe arrival of a stranger is to be expected. The bite of a certain ant\nis lucky (Sect. 22S).\n\n225. The Candle-fly saved the Lost Hunter (C)\n\nFive men fonned themselves into a hunting party, and went out into the forest.\nAt nightfall they built themselves a banab, and next morning they all started in\ndifferent directions to scour the neighborhood. Late in the afternoon they had\nreturned to the resting place, all except one. Three of the four said, \"Our friend is\neither lost or a tiger has eaten him,\" but when they discussed the matter further,\nthey remembered that they had seen no tracks of a tiger throughout the district.\nThe head-man was therefore right when he said, \"No. He must be lost.\" This\nwas really what had happened to the fifth man, who, penetrating deep into the forest,\nwas overtaken by the darkness, which made him miss the track. He wandered on\nand on, and laid himself down under a tree. By and by, a Pu-yu [candle-fly] came\nalong and asked him what he was doing all alone there: when it learned that he had\nlost himself, it offered to show him the way. But the man doubted how such a little\nthing could help him, and it was only when the Candle-fly told him that it intended\nwanning itself at the very fire which his four friends had made at the banab, that\nhe agreed to follow it. And as the two approached the camping-ground, they heard\nthe voices of people talking. \"Listen!\" said the little Fly: \"That's where your\npeople are. We are going there.\" WTien they at last reached the shed, the Candlefly flew in ahead, and told the four men that it was bringing them their lost com-\n)panion; the latter then came in, and his four friends were right glad to see him."
