The young Apalai Indians on the Parou River, Cayenne,\nafter submitting to the mardke (ant and wasp ordeal) must now \"go\nthrough the target test: with their backs turned, they have to throw\ncassava pellets (ioulettes) at a piece of wood upon which a circle has\nbeen traced, and must hit it three times nmning, etc.\" (Cr, 307). In\nits most complete form, however, the shooting ordeal seems to have\nbeen carried out by the Arawaks, and it is from the very old people\nof this people that I have been able to gather the following facts\nconcerning what used to take place in bygone days. When the youth\nwent to his future father-in-law and asked for the girl, the old man\nwould consult his wife and daughter, as a rule, and if everything\nwere satisfactory would say \"yes,\" but would not give him actual\npossession of her until he had performed certain deeds, the first and\nforemost of which was to shoot into a certain woodpecker's nest.\nHe would accordingly ask the suitor whether he were ready or\nwhether he wished to wait a few days. The latter would of course\nsay he was quite ready, so impetuous is youth, and would give a\nminute description of the situation of the particular tree, usually\none close to the water-side, into which he proposed shooting the\narrow. The girl's father, however, would invariably plead some\nexcuse to put him off, say to the next day, and in the meantime would\nget ready a big corial — big enough to carry 10 or 12 men — and engage\nhis crew. When next morning the yoimg man turned up again, the\nold man had everything ready and would get them all into the boat,\nhe himself steering. The girl herself had to sit on the left of her\nwould-be husband in the bows. When within a comparatively short\ndistance from the tree wherein the woodpecker's nest lay concealed,\nthe old man would call upon the crew to pull with all their strength —\nand the young man to draw his bow. Before, however, the arrow\nhad sped, and while yet the bow was fully stretched, the woman had\nto touch his left side with her hand signifying that if his arrow reached\nits mark she agreed to be his. If he missed, the performance had to\nbe postponed to another occasion, he having the right to try as many\ntimes as he liked until he succeeded and in the meantime he might\ncontinue practising on his own accoimt. Luck might assist him on\nthe first occasion, sometimes on the second, third, or fourth, or he\nmight have to make the trial so many times that he would give up the\nattempt as well as all thoughts for the girl, and proceed to some other\nsettlement where the woodpecker's nests were situated to better\nadvantage. Without shooting his arrow into the nest the wooer would\ncertainly never get possession of the girl — neither father nor mother\n\n316 ANIMISM AND FOLK-LOEE OF GUIANA INDIANS [bth. ann. 30\n\nwould give way on that particular point. On the other hand, supposing his aim to have been finally successful, the girl would be as wife\nto him, and he would take up residence in his father-in-law's house.\nThe next thing was for the old Arawak paterfamilias to mark out\na piece of ground, which within so many days the young man to\nwhom he presented an ax for the purpose, had to cut and clear for a\nprovision field. The time specified was usually short, the young man\nhaving to work with might and main, starting early and returning\nlate, but finally completing the task. A similar ordeal was exacted\namong the Makusis and other tribes (ScK, ii, 316). But there was\nstill something else for the Arawak would-be bridegroom to do. For\nduring the time occupied in cutting the field, the old man had busied\nhimself in collecting a large number of crab quakes (baskets), and\nsubsequently he would accompany the lad out to sea, and would\nhimself watch to see that within the one day the youngster really\nfilled all the baskets through his own exertions, and did not obtain\nthe assistance of friends. This completed, the youth became henceforth one of the legal heirs of the house. Should, however, the lad\nnot have cut the field nor filled the requisite number of quakes within\nthe allotted period he would have been laughed and jeered at when\nattending subsequent paiwarris. The two ordeals, just described,\nhowever, were never so essential as that of the shooting of the arrow\ninto the woodpecker's nest.\n\n378. A Warning to Wives (A)"

  "passage_text": "You must remember that in the days of long ago we Arawais would never accept\na suitor for our daughter unless he gave us some proof that he was skilful in the chafe,\nand able to support a wife. Among such tests were those of shooting into a woodpecker's nest from off the bows of a swiftly paddled corial, the filling of so many\nbaskets with crabs during the course of a single tide, and the clearing of a field within\na certain specified period. The first of these was a severe test, it is true, and gradually fell into disuse, though the others were long retained. It was just about the\ntime when the first-mentioned ordeal had been done away with, that a young man,\ncourting a girl, thought he would have no difficulty in gaining permanent possession\nof her, now that all he had to do for his father-in-law was to catch some crabs (Sect.\nS65) and cut a field. So when he went and asked the old man for his daughter and\nobtained his consent, he had no compxmction in settling down at his new quarters,\nfor with us a husband always lives with his bride before he completes the tests: on\ntheir fulfilment, however, will depend his fate — whether he retains permanent possession of her. Two or three weeks having been spent on the honeymoon, the old\nman talked to the lad about going to sea, after the usual manner, to catch crabs,\nand advised him to get his quakes (baskets) ready for a certain day. The youth\nwent into the bush with his companions to cut the necessary mukm [the Creole term\napplied to the material used in weaving baskets], and, on his return, sat down to prepare it (that is, to split it into strands, and to tie them into bundles). As a matter\nof fact, he did not know what else to do with them! And when his comrades, who\nwere already weaving baskets for themselves, saw that he had stopped operations,\nthey inquired the cause, and were told that he intended making. his when he\n\ngot out to sea. (He was ashamed to expose his ignorance of their manufacture.)\n\"You must be very quick at it,\" they said. \"Not at all!\" he replied, \"there\nis no difficulty whatever in the matter. Indeed, I bet that I will make my quakes\nand catch crabs while you are catching yours, and that I will even then beat you.\"\nThey then all made a start: in the corial were the would-be husband, his new\nwife, the old father-in-law, and some five or six other young men. When they\nreached the sea, they anchored their boat at a little distance from the shore, all\nexcept the honeymoon couple getting out, each with a basket, to hunt for crabs.\nAfter they had gone, the young man told his bride to jump out also, and drive aU\nthe little \"four-eye\" fish [TetrophthalmiLS sp.] toward the boat. And while he\nwaa there squatting on the bench, with the mukru strands in his hands trjdng to\nmake his basket, the fish all passed by.' As might have been expected, he realized\nthat he was making no progress, so he made the woman surround the shoal a second\ntime, and drive the fish back again, thus allowing him to have another look. She\nthus continued driving the fish backward and forward, and still he made no progress.\nShe finally became very angry, and picking up one of the quakes out of the corial,\nwaded on to shore: he called out to her to come back, but she took no heed of\nhim. Now the particular quake which she had taken belonged, as she well knew,\nto one of the other men who had accompanied them on the expedition and who was\nan old lover of hers; it was this same man whom she proceeded to join when she\nreached shore. She came close to him, and saying that she wanted to help him, lent\nher assistance in the usual manner : as he dragged the crabs out of their holes, he would\nevery now and then jerk one near her, and she would gather it up into her basket.\nHer husband now came over and joined them, and though he would drag out a crab,\nand throw it toward her, she took not the slightest notice. Although he repeatedly\nshouted, \"Look out! It is escaping. Put it into your basket, \" she would not even\nrecognize him. With her old lover, on the other hand, it was quite different: they\nsoon filled their quakes, and went back to the boat for two more baskets; and these\nwere soon filled. Back to the boat for two more, and so on, backward and forward,\nuntil all the quakes were full. When the husband realized that the others had gathered almost all the crabs that they could possibly carry home with them, he became\ndesperate, and taking his hammock, wrapped within its folds as many of the crustaceans as he could gather. It was now time for them to start on their return journey,\nbut getting into the boat the bride squatted, not on her husband's bench as was the\nproper thing for a recently married young woman to do, but on that of her old lover.\nThe would-be husband said, \"Come here: you are sitting in the wrong place;\" but\nshe and the old man took no notice of the remark, and simply snubbed him. Ftirthermore, when they reached home, all the men tiuiied into their hammocks, while\nthe wife busied herself over the cooking. This did not take very long, as she was\nonly roasting the crabs, so she was soon able to announce, \"Father! It is quite ready\nnow.\" Getting out of his hammock, the old man called the young men up one after\nanother, giving each one his name, and then called SaichiJ Now, on hearing this\nterm of endearment, the husband thought he was intended, and accordingly replied,\nWangj\" [i. e. Yes, thanks, etc.]. \"Xo, no!\" said the old father, \"I mean the\nson-in-law whom I brought in the boat back with me today. He knows how to make\nquakes. You don't.\" Naturally, the erstwhile husband was put to shame, and immediately wended his steps over to his mother's place, carrying with him his hammock\nand the few crabs it contained.   "passage_text": ") The pattern of the weft of these crab-qiiakes is known to the Arawaks as the kassaroa, or \"foar^ye\nflsh,\" from the manner in which the starting strands are arranged, like so many \"eyes.\" The idea\nintended to be conveyed here is that as the man in question did not really know how to make these baskets,\nhe was amcious to get a full view of the flsh, so as to serve him for a model which he could copy.\n\n318 ANIMISM AND FOLK-LOKE OF GUIANA INDIANS [eth. ann. 30\n\ncan, advismg him at the same time that he must wait a while, and be patient, because\nshe was sure the girl would make up to him again. A few days later she took her\nson away to visit am old friend of hers, a man who was very wise in his way. She\ntold this man all her son's troubles, and begged that he wovild teach him not only\nhow to hunt, but also how to make quakes, pegalls, matapis, sifters, and fans, becaiise\nit was due only to her boy's ignorance of these matters that he had lost his wife. The\nold man agreed, for friendship's sake, and mother and son remained with him for more\nthan a year, the latter finally becoming quite as proficient in all the manly arts as\nhis teacher. The result of all this instruction was that when the two of them, after\nleaving the old man's place, returned to their own little house, they never experienced\nthose pangs of hunger that they did in the old times. Each day her son brought home\nsomething, and the babracote was almost groaning under the load of dried meat that it\nnow carried. It happened that a woman passing that way called in one afternoon,\nnoticed all the smoked game, and accepted a choice piece which the old woman offered\nher when she was leaving. Of course, woman-like, she must needs straightway go\nand show this very piece of meat to all the inmates of the house where the faithless\nwife of a year ago was residing, telling her and all her people that her late husband\nwas not such a fool as they had thought: did she not with her own eyes see all the\ngame that he had killed, and all the quakes and matapjs that he had made? Of\ncourse, conversation of this nature, and lota more of it, only made the late wife moiB\nand more anxious to visit the spouse whom she and her father had spumed. And\nthere was good reason for it too. The past year's experience had been a sad one for\nher: she had discovered too late that her second husband was not only worthless, but\nin addition lazy, and that all he was now bent on doing was to lie in his hammock\nall day, and make her work for him. So next morning, she and her mother, telling\ntheir people that they were going for a walk, set out in the direction that led to the\nhouse where lived the master of whose prowess and skill they had heard so much about\nthe day before. They arrived there. The man was lying in his hammock, but his\nmother received them, placed stools, asked them to be seated, and put cassava with\npeppers before them. She also took pains to apologize that there was nothing else\nto offer them, notwithstanding that the babracote with its load of meat was, as' it\nwere, staring at them. The visitors gave a significant look at one another, at the\nbabracote, and at the pepper-jwt with the cassava and peppers: they now felt so\nashamed of themselves at having treated the young man so badly a little more than a\nyear ago that they could not even eat the cassava, and without even touching it,\ntold their hostess to \"take the pot away.\" ' The elder of the two visitors rose to leave,\nand expected her daughter to do the same, but the latter said, \"No! I intend staying\nhere with my first husband; whether he beats me or not, I don't care. He has turned\nout far better than my second one! \" So when her mother had got out of sight, she\nwent up to the hammock where the man was resting, and climbed in, saying, \"I\nhave come back to you, my sweetheart.\" He, however, immediately pushed her\nout, saying, \"I don't want you. I am the lazy, ignorant, and worthless man whom\nyou scorned a year ago.\" She tried again to climb into his hammock, but he would\nnot have her: she spoke \"sweet-mouth\" to him, but he would not listen: crestfallen,\nshe left him, to return to her own people and her second husband, but the first one\nremained alone in his hammock and was glad to hear her go.\n\n378A. I have been unable to confirm Brett's statement as to the\nmembers of the Demarena, a particvJar family group, being restricted\nto connubiiun only with those of the Korobohana family group\n(BrB, 179); otherwise, all the Guiana Indian tribes are exogamous\n\n1 Whenever a visitor comes to a house, he is offered something to eat or drink; to express Ms satisfaction\nat having had enough, he informs his hostess accordingly in this terse maimer.\n\nand trace descent exclusively through the mother. Certainly among\nthe Arawaks and Warraus, sexual union between persons of certain\ndegrees of cousinship is regarded in the same light as is incest by\nEuropeans. (See Sect. 131.)\n\n279. An analysis of the pre-natal and post-natal ordeals undergone by father and mother bring into prominence the fact that they\nbear remarkably strong resemblance to those submitted to at puberty\n(by both sexes) and at menstruation (Sect. £67 et seq.). In the\nmain, these ordeals consist of food restrictions; the tolerance of severe\nphysical pain without visible signs of suffering; and procedures connected with isolation, with water, fire, and cooking. The proper performance of the childbirth ordeals insures that nothing wiU go amiss\nwith the baby. With regard to the food restrictions, before the child's\nbirth, these may be imposed on both parents."

  "passage_text": "Some of the men of the Akawai and Carib nations, when they have reason to expect\nan increase of their families, consider themselves bound to abstain from certain kinds\nof meat, lest the expected child should, in some very mysterious way, be injured by\ntheir partaking of it. The acouri (or agouti) is thus tabooed lest, like that little\nanimal, the child should be meager; the Haimara also, lest it should be blind, the\nouter coating of the eye of that fish suggesting film or cataract; the labba, lest the\ninfant's mouth should protrude like the labba's, or lest it be spotted like the labba,\nwhich spots would ultimately become ulcers. The marudi is also forbidden, lest\nthe infant be still-bom, the screeching of that bird being considered ominous of death.\n[Br, 355.]\n\nAmong the Pomeroon Arawaks, though the killing and eating\nof a snake duriog the woman's pregnancy is forbidden to both father\nand mother the husband is allowed to kill and eat any other animal.\nThe cause assigned for the taboo of the snake is that the httle infant\nmight be similar, that is, able neither to talk nor to walk. Neither\nparent, however, when carrying a piece of cassava cake, may either\nturn it over in the hand, or curl it up at the sides ; otherwise, the ears\nof the child, when born, wiU be found curled over. Any game hunted\nby dogs is strictly forbidden the pregnant woman of this tribe, just\nas it is at her menstruation; otherwise the dog would be spoiled for\nhunting purposes, permanently in the latter circumstances, temporarily in the former, the dog recovering its powers only when the\nbaby was born. Hence, when a man brings home any animal that\nhas been hunted by a dog, it is his wife's business to see that it is\nnot partaken of by any woman in either of the states named.\nAn interesting reference to this belief will be found in TimeTiri (vol.\nII, 1883, p. 355), in which report is made of a woman's wages being\nstopped because, while weediag; she partook of the game caught by\na hunting dog and so rendered tbe dog useless. She is forbidden to\neat when pregnant any \"big meat,\" as turtle or tapir, or fish that\nhas much blood in it, as at menstruation; she can now eat only the\ntail portion of a fish. Infringement of any of these rules will result\n\n320 ANIMISM AND POLK-LOEE OF GUIANA INDIANS [eth. ANN. 30\n\nin something being amiss with the child when born. The Indians of\nthe Uaupes River, Rio Negro, \"believe that if a woman, during her\npregnancy, eats of any meat, any other animal partaking of it will\nsuffer; if a domestic animal or tame bird, it will die; if a dog, it will\nbe for the future incapable of hunting; and even a man will ever\nafter be unable to shoot that particular kind of game\" (ARW, 349) :\nhence, meat has to be avoided by her. A Pomeroon Arawak female\nwiU beget twins through eating any double fruit during the period of\nher pregnancy. The SaHva husband, however (G, i, 189), regarded\nsuch a result as a sure sign of his wife's disloyalty, believing that only\none of the twins could possibly be his. Another pregnancy restriction\non the Pomeroon is that the Arawak woman must not laugh, and\nmust not grieve; 'neither may she look at the face of a dead person\nthough it is permissible for her to gaze on the body.\n\n380. And even when the baby does put in an appearance, the\nmother's troubles, like the father's, are far from over; for until her\nyoungster is able to walk well, the Arawak mother on the Pomeroon\nmust eat neither deer, furtle, nor iguana, animals which, for some\ndays after birth, creep or crawl very slowly, in contradistinction, for\ninstance, from the bush-hog, that will start to rim directly it has\nlittered. The idea is that by eating such flesh the mother will cause\nher infant to walk too slowly. On the islands, the Carib mother\nabstained from female crabs, which would give the child stomachache, while the father had to avoid certain animals for fear of\nthe youngster participating in their natural faults. If a father\nate tiu-tle, the child would be heavy, and have no brains; if he ate a\nparrot, the child would have a parrot nose; if a crab, the consequence would be long legs (BBR, 248-9). The mainland Caribs of\nCayenne (Galibis) avoided deer, hog, and other large game (PBa,\n223-4). Brett, in a quotation apparently from McClintock, says that\nthe Akawai, Carib, and Warrau husband abstains from venison\nafter his wife's delivery for the same reason that the Arawak mother\nshuns it (Br, 356). The Roucouyenne father must eat no fish or game\nthat has been caught with an arrow, but must content himself with\ncassava and with small fish that have been poisoned with the \"nicou\"\nplant; should he disregard this taboo the child will either soon die\nor develop vicious propensities. For the Carib Islander, paternity\nmust undoubtedly have proved somewhat trying; for ten or twelve\ndays he had \"to take to his bed,\" and subsist on a little cassava\nand water; he ate only of the insides of the cassava cakes, leaving\nthe outsides for the subsequent feasting; for from 6 to 10 or 12\nmonths later he had to abstain from several meats, as manati, turtle,\nhog, fowl, and fish, for fear of hurting his infant, but such extreme\nfasting was carried out only at the birth of the first male child."

  "passage_text": "When the fasting period was approaching its conclusion, he had to
submit to a scarification, by means of agouti teeth, upon his shoulders
without a murmur, and the better he bore this infliction the more
vahant would his son prove; the blood thus made to flow was not
allowed to fall onto the ground, but was smeared on the child's face
to make it courageous {ginereux) (RoP, 550). The actual termination of the fast must here have been celebrated more or less ceremoniously: "Placed on a red-painted seat, the women bring him
food, which the old men put in his mouth, as they would do to a child,
the cassava and the fish being in small pieces; he eats the cassava, but
ejects the fish after chewing it. He would become sick if he began to
eat too well at once; he is made to drink by being held by the neck"
(BBR, 249). The scarification and fiogging ordeals of puberty, are
repeated on the Carib father, both island and mainland, after his wife's
deUvery of either boy or girl : the reputed idea is " to transfer his courage
(muih) to the children" (ScR, ii, 431). In the former case, after a
coiirse of very limited diet he is "brought to a public place, looking
like a skeleton, and standing upright on two large flat cakes of cassavas.
The sponsors then begin to scratch and cut his skin with very sharp
agouti teeth. They first begin on the sides, then the shoiilders, from
the arm to the elbow, from elbow to wrist, and from the thighs to the
ankles. . . . He is then painted and rubbed with roucou leaves,
pepper seeds and tobacco juice, and placed on a red-painted seat"
(BBR, 248-9), and fed, as already mentioned. The Mainland Carib,
the Galibi of Cayenne, after some weeks' subsistence on a stinted diet,
is "scarified on various parts of the body with fish-bones or agouti
teeth: very often even he is given several lashes with a whip"
(PBa, 223-4).

381. After the birth of the baby come the various procedures connected with the isolation of one or both parents; in the case of the
father, his so-called "lying-in" is spoken of as the couvade, and is
met with in many tribes, for example, Arawaks, Warraus, Caribs
(who call the practice Icenonimdno) , Makusis, and Wapisianas. In
the case of the Mainland Caribs (Ca3^enne) "when their wives are
confined for the first time, the newly married husband has to sling
his hammock high up to the ridge of the house" (PBa, 223-4).
With the Island Caribs, if the child is a firstborn male, the husband, as soon as the woman is delivered, goes to bed, complains
and acts as though he had been dehvered (BBR, 248), and submits
to a restricted diet, etc. As with the Caribs, so with the Arawaks
and Warraus, it is practically the husband who is isolated, and does
the "lying-in." Indeed, in these three tribes, the woman is isolated
only during actual delivery, which takes place either out in the bush,
in a separate shelter, or in a compartment specially partitioned off from

15061°— 80 ETH— 15 21

322 ANIMISM AND FOLK-LOEE OF GUIANA INDIANS [ets. ANN. 30

the rest of the house. With the bath that she takes within a comparatively few hours after the interesting event has occurred, her
isolation, and with it any dangerous influence of her recent condition,
ceases. The woman is her own accoucheuse; even during the night
and in wet season she will leave the house and retire to a secluded'
spot near by. She occupies herself with her daily affairs imtil the
last moment: she may come home with a quake containing the baby
instead of the usual cassava; and '.'on the morrow she is prepared
to undertake all the indoor work of the household" (Da, 248). Confinement takes place either in the forest or in some little hut; she is
always alone unless some difficulty presents itseK, when an old woman,
will attend (PBa, 226). With the Makusis and Wapisianas, both
parents engage in a "lying-in" for a shorter or longer period after
the appearance of baby. The Makusi father takes to his hammock,
placed near that of his wife, until the navel-string falls off; but before
doing this, if he has no separate building, he will prepare a palm-leaf
partition in the hut (ScR, ii, 314). When the partition was finished,
the [Wapisiana] husband himg up in it both his own and his wife's
hammock, and therein they lay to "take to bed" {die Wochen zu
Mlten) like the Makusis (ScR, ii, 389). During the Ijdng-in of the
mother, or couvade of the father, they are considered equally unclean,
such uncleanness being occasionally regarded as persisting for long
afterward. Thus, the Mainland Carib (in Cayenne) is obUged to devote
himself to the service of an old Indian and to leave his wife for some
months; during this period he has to be submissive and regard himself
as a real slave (PBa, 223-4). When in couvade a visitor enters his
house, that visitor's dogs will soon die (Cr, 241). The Arawaks and
Warraus say that if a man during the period he ought to remain in
couvade indulges in sexual relations with any woman other than his
wife, the infant will die through inabihty to exert its emunctory powers.
After hghting her fire and supplying her with drinking cups it is the
duty of the female Wapisiana population to keep as far away from
the lying-in woman as possible for the few days that she is deemed

  "passage_text": "XJraima once had La hia possession a bird's egg, which he kept in a calabash; he
took great care of it until it should hatch out. He met two girls on the road: they
saw the egg and asked him to let them have it. "Nol" he said, "I can not." They
worried and even followed him, but he still refused. So they seized the e^, and
in the course of the scuffle broke it. Uraima then spoke to the women as follows:
"Since you have done this, trouble will follow you from now onward. Up to the
present, the egg has belonged to man. For the future it will belong to woman and
she will have to hatch it." It is only the female that lays eggs nowadays.

282. There seem to be some curious restrictions concerning water,
so far as the father is concerned, both previous and subsequent to birth.
R. L. Kingston gives the following interesting pre-natal example:
"While some (True) Caribs were poisoning the upper Pomeroon
with haiari for fish, I saw one of them rub his shins with the beaten
and washed-out haiari. Asking why he did this, he told me his wife
was with child, and that he could not therefore go into the water
without first rubbing his legs with haiari, lest aU the fish should sink
to the bottom" [instead of floating narcotized on the surface] (Ti, n,
1883, p. 355). It was said to be a custom of the Island Caribs
that "they often deUver near the fire, and the chUd is bathed at
once; but a funny precaution is, that if it is bom at night, the men
who are sleeping in the house go and bathe so that the child may not
catch cold" (BBR, 248-9). It is curious that the Pomeroon Arawak
women will not bathe their infants until such time as the navelstring heals, for fear of the same contingency happening. On the
other hand, his usual bath is forbidden the Makusi father (ScR, ii,
314) during his time of couvade. Strange to say, it is the bath which
in most tribes constitutes the final piuification of the mother, at the
end of her lying-in period, whether such period be of a few hours' or
several days' duration: Beyond what has already been mentioned
concerning fire — how some women (Island Caribs) wiU often dehver
near a fire and how others will apparently have one hghted for
them — I have found no further references to childbirth in connection
with fire, except one in connection with the navel-string. Bancroft
is the only author who speaks of the division of "the umbilie vessels,
which they do with a brand of fire, which cauterizes their orifices,
and renders a ligatmre unnecessary" (Ba, 330). Two old Arawak
women are my authority for saying that in the old days the cord was
burned off with a heated nail. Cooking for a man is strictly prohibited to a pregnant woman: she may however "clean" the meat, but
in cleaning any animal or fish she must not cut off the ears, nails, or
fins. In this latter connection there is a curious prohibition concerning fingernails in force among the Makusis : neither men nor women
at times of couvade or lying-in must scratch their bodies or heads

324 ANIMISM AND FOLK-LORE OF GUIANA INDIANS [eth. ANN. 30

with their nails. A piece of the midrib of the kokerite pahn is
specially employed for the purpose (ScK, ii, 314).

283. In many of the tribes during the couvade, and often for long
afterward, the husband is prohibited from engaging in certain of his
ordinary occupations. The Pomeroon Arawak must neither smoke,
lift any heayy weight, use a fish-hook, nor have intimate relations
with any woman. The Mainland Carib of Cayenne was not allowed
to cut any big timber with an ax (PBa, 223-4). The Makusi must
not touch his weapons (ScR, ii, 313). Should these and similar prohibitions be not observed, some evil would be sure to befall the child.
There is another interesting example recorded of a man ( ?Arawak)
during couvade lying in his hammock and twisting a new bowstring;
baby. began to scream, with the result, that the father had to undo
the whole hne (Ti, ii, 1883, p. 355).

When one reahzes what the Indian conception of child-life is, the
explanation of the above otherwise extraordinary customs becomes
comparatively simple. In its material as weU as in its spirit nature
the baby is beheved to be part and parcel of both parents, and even
at birth is not considered to have an independent existence. Its
material dependence on the father ceases only when the navel-string
is finally detached, the signail for the male parent to conclude his
"hatching" or couvade. The baby's spirit nature does not, however, usually free itself from the mother until the lapse of many
months, when it begins to crawl or walk (an occasion which in some
tribes seems to have been celebrated by a festival, with hair cutting
and other features) ; hence, all this time, whatever can aflfect the
mother in the way of food, or otherwise, exerts a corresponding influence on the child. On the other hand, its spirit nature may occasionally tend to wander all on its own account. Thus, when a Monica
River woman is carrying her very young infant along a pathway and
happens to meet a cross path, she will break off a leaf or two from
an adjoining bush, and throw it on the latter; baby's Spirit must
follow her and not go off in another direction. On the conclusion of
the couvade the baby's spirit nature, though physically freed from
the Spirit of the father, and in that sense independent of it, nevertheless accompanies the father for a similar period, that is, until it
can crawl, and can be influenced by it so long as the companionship,
so to speak, is retained. When the infant begins to crawl, its hair
is cut for the first time. Rev. Mr. Dance was, I beUeve, among the
first to appreciate fuUy the true signification of these facts in connection with, presumably, the Arawaks. I myself have had opportimities for studying them among Arawaks as well as Warraus."

  "passage_text": "The infant Spirit clings to the father, gazes upon him, follows him wherever he
goes, and for the time being is as intimate and familiar with the father, as he is with
his own infant body with which the infant Spirit is only recently associated. How

then can the father ... go out to the forest or field to use an ax or cutlass, when
the Spirit of the child which follows him as a second shadow might be between the
ax and the wood? How cUmb a tree, if the infant spirit is also to essay the climbii^,
and fall, perhaps to the injury of the infant lying in the hammock? How hunt when
the arrow might pierce the accompanying spirit of the child, which would be death
to the little mortal at home? If, traveling through the woods you happen to meet a
tairu leaf, which is formed very much in shape of a corial, floating on a stream or pond
of water, and furnished with a tiny wooden seat and paddle, cut out and placed therein:
or should you, in stepping over a fallen tree discover two sticks each placed from the
ground to the trunk of the tree, disturb them not. . . . When the father wades through
the water, the toddling spirit . . . must paddle over in the taini-leaf boat: and when
his sire crosses over the stump, the little temporary bridge enables the infantile Spirit
to cUmb over. . . But notwithstanding the greatest vigilance, the little Spirit is
sometimes lost, and then the body pines and dies if the Piai doctor is not fortunate
enough to recover it. [Da, 249.]

For my own part, I am very much inclined to believe that this
little Baby Spirit is identical with the Familiar Spirit (Sect. 93 A).

284. In view of the facts mentioned throughout this chapter it is
as well to note that, on the Orinoco, when an infant (male or female)
was bom with any defect or monstrosity it was put to death (G, ii,
60). Similar procedure was in vogue in Cayenne (PBa, 227), while
Schomburgk states that "the shocking practice of destroying
deformed children is not so general among the savages of Guayana
as has been supposed" (ScF, 219). On the Amazon there was the
curious custom of killing all the first-bom children among the Xim&-
nas and Cauxanas, tribes met with between the Ifa and Japura
Rivers (ARW, 355) . Among the Zaparos of the Napo River (upper
Amazon), when a mother having a very young child dies, the child
is sometimes buried ahve (Sect. 76) with her (AS, 175). On the
Orinoco, among the Sahvas, twins were considered a sign of dishonor.

They call the mother nicknames; some say that she is of the rodent family, which
bear little rats four at a time, etc. Directly a Saliva savage gives birth to a baby and
feels that still another remains, she will bury the first rather than put up with the jokes
and chafSng of her neighbors, or merit the frown with which her husband regards it.
The husband's view is that only one of those twins can possibly be his; the presence
of the other is a sure sign of his wife's disloyalty. One of the Indian captains gives his
wife a whipping in public for having dared to bring forth twins; and warns the other
women -as to the serious beating he will give them if they do the same. [G, i, 189.]

The same thing takes place on the River Cuduiary, among the
Kob6was, at the present day, the second-bom of the twins being
killed, but if of different sexes, the girl is sacrificed (KG, ri, 146).

!384A. There are certainly traces of a belief in sexual relationships
having no necessary connection with the production of children.
Even at the present day women can cohabit with Water Spirits
without disastrous consequences resulting (Sect. 186). On the
other hand women can get babies if they want them, by eating certain
binas, plant or animal (Sects. 237, 238) ; in a case of this kind the

326 ANIMISM AND FOLK-LOEE OF GUIANA INDIANS [eth. ANN. 30

child is already in existence, its body being attached to, and by some
mysterious means passing into, the body of the mother. As to the
origin of such babies, aU I can gather is that they arrive in the water or
in the bush, and hence may make their appearance in our mundane
world either as a gift from the Water Spirits (Sect. 186), or at the
instigation of the Spirits of the Forest (Sects. 117, 302), with or
without the agency of the piai. The following is a Warrau story
bearing on this subject;

The Little Bush Child (W)

A long time ago it was customary for a woman, when she yearned for a child, to
wander about in the forest until she found one. It so happened that a certain woman,
Yaburawdko, in going to her field found a little child on the road — a pretty boy he
was — and she brought hiTn home. She minded him, and he had sense enough to call
her "Mdma. " By and by, however, the child got mischievous, and made her vexed.
She said, "You have really nothing to do with me; so why should you annoy me?"
The husband remonstrated with her, expressing himself to her somewhat as follows:
"You must not be angry with the child, but must mind him carefully. " She continued, however, to be cross with the boy, and finally ill-treated him. "I am not
going to be bothered with you any more," she exclaimed. "You have nothing to
do with me. You are not mine. You don't belong to me. " With this, the child
disappeared, whereupon the husband said: "Well, he's gone now, but he will come
back again, and this time enter youi body, and you will have trouble enough to get
rid of him. " Sure enough, after a time the child did enter her womb, and, oh ! the
trouble and the pains she suffered before she was delivered of him. Women ever
since have borne children in this manner just because Yaburaw&o was so unkind
to the little bush child."
}

Apprenticeship and Installation (297).\n\nPower over Spirits: of animals (298), of himself (e.g. invisibility) and of other\nIndians (299).\n\nAs interpreter of dreams (SOO); seer or prophet (SOI); his general versatility (SOg-\nSOS); guardian of the tribal traditions (S04); the giver of personal names (SOS); his\ntreatment of sickness and disease (S06).\n\nDisease and treatment: signification (507); usual treatment by Arawak piai (SOS);\nby Carib (S09); by Galibi (SIO); by ?Oyampi (Sll); by Makusi (S12); by Indians of\nCaracas (SIS); by Carib Islanders (SH). Spirits specially invoked in cure (S15);\nobjects extracted from patients (5i6) ; dieting of patient's relatives and family (577);\nmedical fees (S18); Quack doctors (S19).\n\n385. There is abundant evidence that the medicine-men practised\nwhat they preached, and had every confidence in the powers with\nwhich they had been intrusted. \"They practise those incantations\nover their own sick children, and cause them to be practised over\nthemselves when sick\" (BrA, 117). \"They act the farce on themselves when they are disordered: a practice which has not a little\ncontributed to overthrow aU doubts of the sincerity of their pretensions\" (Ba, 314). \"The piai himself beheves in it: one will put himself in the hands of another when sick\" (Go, 13). Schomburgk was\n\"convinced that the piai bfelieves in the eflScacy of his witchcraft aa\nfirmly as his proteges\" (ScR, n, 146). The real causes of the existing\nprejudice against the medicine-men are not far to seek, and have\noften been clearly expressed. \"As doctors, augurs, raui-makers,\nspeU-binders, leaders of secret societies, and depositaries of the tribal\ntraditions and wisdom, their influence was generally powerful. Of\ncourse it was adverse to the Europeans, especially the missionaries,\nand also of coiu^e it was generally directed to their own interest or\nthat of their class; but this is equally true of priestly power wherever it gains the ascendency, and the injm-ious effect of the Indian\nshamans on their nations was not greater than has been in many\ninstances that of the Christian priesthood on European communities\"\n\n328 ANIMISM AND FOLK-LOKE OF GUIANA INDIANS [bth. ann. 30\n\n(Bri, 55) . On the other hand, there is not a single recorded instance\nof the Guianese Indian priesthood ever having submitted those of\ntheir people holding religious Views different from their own to either\ntorture or the block. The Warrau word for the priest-doctor is\nvnshidatu (wisiddd, according to Brett), similarly applied to the\nkickshaws. In some of the Orinoco nations, they call these men\nMojan: in others Piache: iu others AlabuqUi, etc. (G, ii, 25).\nThe Piapocos Indians of the lower Guaviar River speak of them as\nKamarikeri (Cr, 526) ; the Caribs of the lower Caroni River as Marirri\n(AVH, III, 89), and the Island Caribs as Bove (RoP, 473). The\nArawak designation is of equal iaterest and also of extended range:\nit is Semi-tcMchi or Semi-cihi, the same term applied generally to\nthe kickshaws and various apparatus employed in the pursuit of the\ncraft (Sect; 93)."

the Barima River, came upon the burial-place of an Indian Peaiman
or Medicine-man. The house imder which the burial had been made
was hung round with five of the typical peaiman's rattle or shak-shak,
and over the grave itself was placed the box of the dead man, containing the various objects which had been the instmments, or credentials, of his calling. The contents of this box . . . were a carved
wooden doll or baby." The doll, or manikin (fig. 5), which I saw
used for the purpose on the Monica River, was a Uttle black one
about 2i inches long, balanced "gingerly" on its feet, which bore
traces of having been touched with some gummy substance : if during
the course of the special incantation it remained in the erect position,
the patient would recover, but if it fell over, this would be a sure
sign of his approaching death. In parts of Cayenne the doll is
replaced by the Anaan-tanha, or Devil-figure (Sect. 311), which is
unmercifully thrashed with a view to compdling the Evil Spirit to

leave the invalid. The identity of this mainland doll, or manikin,
with the idol, or cemi, of the Antilleans has already been indicated

291. The crystals are employed for charming, bewitching, or
cm-sing others, though the references in the literatm:e to their application in this manner are exceedingly scarce. Indeed, I can call
to mind only the following from Cr6vaux (554): "I notice on the
neck of one of them [Guahibos of the Orinoco] a bit of crystal set in
the cavity of an alligator's tooth. The whole has the name of
guanare. ... It is with this guanare that the Guahibos throw speUs
(jgrtenidessortiZegres) on theirhated neighbors, the Piaroas. . . . Every
mineral that presents in its lines and shape a certain regularity is to

them the wojk of a devil or a sorcerer."
Cursing and similar procedure are not, however, the sole prerogative of the medicineman, at least not in the Pomeroon District
of the present day; the procedure is known
as Tw-a to both Warraus and Arawaks, and
is practised, I am told, by very old people.
As a remedy for over-fatigue, Schombiirgk
describes "Macusis and Wapisianas cutting
each other's legs with a piece of rock crystal,
an instrument to which they ascribed particular virtue, refusing instead of it my offer of
a lancet'' (ScF, 235).

in spells, they make httle decorated instruments, of tender rushes about a foot long,
which their physicians or priests called Pyeis
employ, together with other magical implements, as wands to drive out these demons
of 111." These instruments I have been unable to identify thus far.
Finally, on the authority of the old medicine-man who taught me
the greater part of what I Itnow concerning the practice of the art,
a "charm" of some description was worn on the chest suspended
by a cord hung round the neck (Sect. 93). The one that my late
teacher (Bariki) employed is flat and oval, made of some resinous
material, and ornamented on one side with the incised figure o^ a
female frog (fig. 6) . It had been given Bariki by his grandfather when
the latter taught him his profession, and when the old man died, he
left it to me. In the extract from Timehri (1892, p. 184) above

representation, in reddish quartz, of a dog sitting on its haunches

circumstances, to suppose that this object was the doctor's chestornament just referred to. There is absolutely no evidence of any
Guiana Indian toy being u§ed in this manner, and it is ridiculous to
beheve that the vast amount of labor necessarily involved in carving

medicine-man appears to

to have passed to the eldest
son(Ba,316). Ifhehasno

172), although the same

elsewhere states that, under

chooses the craftiest among
the boys (ScR, i, 423-4) . It
is likely that the secrets
and mysteries of the profession may also have been
imparted to outsiders for a consideration. I happen to have known
one of the fraternity who taught another his profession for the sum
down of eleven doUars together with the gift of his daughter. Im
Thurn (334) says: "If there was no son to succeed the father,
the latter chose and trained some boy from the tribe — one with an
epileptic tendency being preferred. ... It has been said that epileptic subjects are by preference chosen as piaimen, and are trained
to throw themselves at wiU into convulsions." Perhaps this idea had
its origin in the fact that through the use of a narcotic powder, the
piais can throw themselves into a condition of wild ecstasy (ScR,
I, 423-4) : several such powders were known to some of the Guiana
Indians, as the Yufa (G, r, 181), etc. On the other hand I can find
no references in the hteratm-e to the choice of epileptic subjects;
furthermore, the unlikehhood is turned into impossibility, when it is
borne in mind that the victim of such a convulsion would be unconscious during its progress.

very nose of the unsuspecting Father. On the authority of Joseph
Stoll, Aiawak, catechist at St. Bede's Mission, Barama River, young

there was in each settlement one special building for the use of aU
these doctors : " There is a certain house devoted to the use of these
sorcerers, in which they perform their superstitious exercises, and
converse with the Devil."

So the four\nparents started in search of the two little ones, and went to a neighbor's house, where\nthey saw them playing with a third child, Kdwai-wari. But the same thing happened at this house as at the previous one — the parents all got into conversation, and\nforgot their real business until finally they found all three children missing. It was\na case now of six parents searching for three infants; but at the end of the first day\nthe third couple abandoned the search, and at the end of the second day the second\ncouple did likewise. In the meantime the three children had wandered on and on,\nmaking friends with the marabuntafl [wasps], which in those days talked but did\nnot sting. It was these children that told the black ones to sting people, and the red\nones to give them fever in addition. And it was when the children arrived at the\nseashore that the first pair of parents met them. However, by this time they were\nchildren no more, but big boys. I will not go back.\" But when both father and\nmother implored him with tears to return, he relented, and promised them that if\nthey built a proper heburhanohu [lit. But in those days we had\nnone of this plant here : it grew far away out in an island over the sea. I do not know\nwhether this island was Trinidad, or not, but we Warraus call it Nibo-yuni [lit. Manwithout] because it was peopled entirely by women [cf. Sect. 3SS], according to\nwhat the old people tell us. He ran to his Aijamo [head-man, chief] and said: \"There is a man who has\nan object with which he nearly kUled me and I must get my payment [i. e. my\n•revenge]. I am going back to kill him.\" \"All right!\" said the Aijamo, \"I will go\nwith you.\" So they went together, and brought sickness to a friend and neighbor of\nKomatari's; for they were afraid of attacking Komatari himself. However, his sick\nfriend sent for him. Komatari went, and played the maraka on him, and took out\nhis sickness. So the killing Hebu made another man ill, but Komatari took the\ndisease out of him also. The Hebu next afflicted a third victim, and again Komatari\nwas victorious. But when he attacked a fourth one, Komatari was out hunting.\nWhen he returned, the poor fellow was in a bad enough condition: so strong did the\nsickness come, that Komatari could not cure him — he had \"stood too long.\" The\nkilling Hebu then explained to Komatari that it would always be thus: some patients\nhe (Komatari) could save, and other patients he could not. Of course Komatari had\nbeen able to find out the names of all the Hebus that had lent him assistance in the\nmanufacture of his maraka, and it is to these different Hebus whom the present-day\nmedicine-men are said to \"sing\" and call on when they cure the sick. For instance,\nthe name of the Hebu that procured the tobacco seeds for Komatari was Wau-uno\n[=Arawak Anura], \"the white crane.\"\n\n397. Tlie apprenticeship of tlie medicine-man in the olden days was\nvery far from being the proverbial bed of roses. Among other tests,\nhe had for many months to practise self-denial, and submit under\na stinted diet to the prohibition of what were to him accustomed\nluxuries. He had to satisfy his teacher in his knowledge of the\ninstincts and habits of animals, in the properties of plants, and the\nseasons for flowering and bearing, for the piai man was often consulted as to when and where game was to be found, and he was more\nthan often correct in his surmises. He also had to know of the\ngrouping of the stars into constellations, and the legends connected\nnot only with them, but with his own tribe. He had likewise to be\nconversant with the media for the invocation of the Spirits, as chants\nand recitatives, and also to be able to imitate animal and human\nvoices. He had to submit to a chance of death by drinking a decoction of tobacco in repeated and increasing doses, and to have his eyes\nwashed with the infusion of hiari leaves (Sect. 169); he slowly\nrecovered, with a confused mind, believing that in his trance, the\neffect of narcotics and a distempered mind, he was admitted into the\ncompany of the Spirits, that he conversed with them, and was by themselves consecrated to the office of piai priest-doctor (Da, 285).\nBancroft (316) says that the novitiate \"is dosed with the juice\nof tobacco till it no longer operates as an emetic.\" Sometimes, as\namong the Oyambis on the Oyapock River in French Guiana, other\nthings were mixed with the tobacco, for example, a plant called\n\nquinquiva, as well as certain of the drippings from an exposed dead\nbody (Cr, 158). For the same colony Fathers Grillet and Bechamel\n(GB, 48) record that the medicine-men proffer neither physic nor\ndivination \"till they have made divers experiments, one of which\nis so dangerous that it often makes them burst. They stamp the\ngreen leaves of tobacco and squeeze out the juice of it, of which they\ndrink the quantity of a large glassfxil,*etc.; so that none but those\nwho are of a very robust constitution, who try this practice upon\nthemselves, escape with their lives.\" Brett (Br, 362) also testifies\nto the severity of the ordeal, for after the novice has been reduced to\nthe deathlike state of sickness to which the fasting coupled with the\ndrinking of tobacco-water has brought him —\n\nHiB death is loudly proclaimed, and his countrymen called to witness his state.\nRecovery is slow, and about the tenth day he comes forth from the sacred hut in a\nmost emaciated condition. For ten months after the new sorcerer must abstain from\nthe flesh of birds and beasts, and only the smallest kinds of fish are allowed him. They belonged to a species which the Makusi Indians\ncalled wampang; the Wapisiana camuiba. The hives or nests are\ngenerally fixed to branches of trees, and are from 2 to 3 feet in\nlength. ... It stings severely; and in order to secure nests, the\nIndians kindle fires under them, when the insects abandon their fabrics\nen masse. I have, however, seen an Indian who was the conjurer or\npiaiman of his tribe, merely approach the nest, and knocking with\nhis fingers against it, drive out all the bees without a single one\ninjuring him. I noticed him drawing his fingers under the pits of\nhis arms before he knocked against the hive\" (ScT, 40). The piai\nsystem made a secret art of hunting; from the priest-doctor the\nhimters learned to hunt for the particular game they required, and\nreceived at his hands charms — maklar and hina — to insure their\nsuccess (Da, 251). Among the Indians of the Uaupes River, the\npiais are believed to have power to destroy dogs or game and to\nmake the fish leave a river (ARW, 347). The medicine-man furthermore coiold transform himself into an animal (Sect. 154) ) if 1^ wife\nbecomes pregnant she may bear him a tiger, an animal into which\nhe himself may be transformed at death (KG, ii, 154).\n\n299. Certainly among many of the tribes the \"doctors\" were believed\nto be endowed with such power over their own spirits as to render\nthemselves invisible. At a Makusi village on the Karakarang River,\na branch of the Cotinga, Barrington Brown (Bro, 119) was told that\nmany of their people had gone to Roraima to see an Indian sorcerer\nthere who had the power of making himseK invisible at will. Thus, im Thurn (339) :\n\"He is able to call to him and question the spirit of any sleeping\nIndian of his own tribe, so that if an Indian wishes to know what an\nabsent friend is doing, he has only to employ the piai-man to summon\nand question the spirit of the far-away Indian. Or the piai-man may\nsend his own spirit, his body remaining present, to get the required\ninformation.\"\n\n300. The piai's reputation as an interpreter of dreams was second to\nnone: he was both dreamer and seer (Sect. 298), but this is only what\n\n342 ANIMISM AND FOLK-LOEE OF GUIANA INDIANS [dth. ANN. 30\n\nmight have been expected, considering the powers he possessed over\nother people's Spirits (Sect. 299), and dreams are really but people's\nSpirits (Sect. 86).\n\nSaved by a Dream (W)*"

At last there was so much contention, that the husband was\nobliged to send the younger one away, and she took her baby with her. He had no\nbad mind toward her, but he could not stand the continual quarreling. When taking\nher departure, he gave her a sharp knife with which to protect herself on the road.\nThe poor woman wandered on imtil nightfall, when she came upon a fine ite [Mauritia]\npalm; cutting a forked stick, sheplanted it against the tree, and climbed on it. Takiug\nthe youngest aa-yet-imopened leaf, she spread it out and made a sort of tempoiajy\nbasket of it, into which she coiled herself together with her baby, and there she tried\nto sleep. Now, upon this particular palm, the fruit was plentiful — some seven or\neight bunches — and around the stalk of each bunch she had taken the precaution of\ncutting a little ring, so that with the slightest touch, any bunch would- fall to the\nground. Somehow or other, the unhappy mother could not sleep, and late in the\nnight she heard the growling of the tigers who had been attracted by her scent. One\nof these brutes climbed the palm and jxmiped on one of the fruits, but no sooner had\nhe touched it than it gave way and he fell with a crash into the very midst of hia\nfellows below who, believing him to be the woman they were in search of, promptly\ntore him to pieces. Another tiger made a similar attempt, climbed the tree, jumped\non the fruit, and ended in the same disastrous manner. And so with a third, fourth,\nfifth, and sixth tiger — all were similarly destroyed. By this time the dawn had broken,\nand the carcasses Were left rotting at the bottom of the tree. What a sight for the terrified\nmother nestling up above! She could see all the tigers lying still and quiet, but was\nafraid to come down lest they might still be alive. She therefore waited a little and\nwhen, after the rising of the sun, she recognized a wasp settling on each of their protruded tongues, she knew that the tigers must all be dead and could now do her no\nharm. As soon as she got down she continued her journey, and wandering along all\nday, she arrived about nightfall at a big manicole tree, which she climbed, with the\nbaby fastened on her back. Tigers were likewise very prevalent here, and scenting\nher presence, they started digging around the roots with the result that by and by,\nthe tree fell with a crash, but fortunately into an immense spider-web, where its living\nfreight became stuck. Now the woman's father was a celebrated piai, and while the\nfirst night's occurrences were taking place, he was dreaming all about her and the\ntigers. Next morning he started to search and came upon her while resting in the\nspider-web. It was owing to the baby making water that he had cause to look up\najid discover his daughter. By daylight he had shot the tigers that were prowling\naround, and then helped down the woman and his grandchild. Both daughter and\nfather cried; the former had been so strongly punished, the latter was so glad to have\nher home again.\n\n301. Among other duties that the medicine-men might be called\non to perform was to fix the time most propitious for the people to\nattack their enemies (HWJtJ, 244). They were supposed to be gifted\nwith the power of prophecy: they foretold the issue of battles (BBR,\n234), whether there would be war or peace; similarly, they could\nprophesy as to the crops — whether these would prove scanty or\nabundant (FD, 51).\n\n' For anotber Warrau Tersion of this story, see Sect. 1S6A .\n\n302. The Pomeroon Arawaks appear to credit the piai with being\nable to influence the Yawahus in bringing the as-yet-Tmbom babes to\nthe mothers (Sect. 28^). In some districts, as on the Berbice, the\npiais were said to be professional poisoners, but it must be remembered that the charge of poisoning was one made against all Arawaks as a habit (Da, 16). Among the wurali-poison-making tribes,\nfor example, the Makusis, Bemau's statement (Be, 36) that the\n\"conjurers alone are conversant with the art of compounding it\"\ndoes not seem to be borne out by the facts. At one place on the\nOrinoco, as already stated (Sect. 297), the sorcerers were alleged to\nbe rendered poison-proof (G, n, 25). Waterton's statement (W, 223)\nthat \"he is an enchanter: he finds out things lost\" is only a fiurther\nexample of the piai's supposed versatility. I remember on one\noccasion unconscioiisly giving great offence to my old doctor-friend,\nBariki, now alas! gone to his long, last rest, by asking him ■!/ he knew\nso-and-so: he gave me a withering glance, and after a few moments,\nsilence, said, \"I know all things.\" Taking the hint, I subsequently\ninvariably sought information from him by putting my question in\nthe form of \"Tell me this, or that,\" with the result that, pleased\nwith my appreciation of his mental superiority, he was always ready\nto impart all he knew, and perhaps more.\n\n303.   "passage_text": "1 Before contact with European inBuences, it was strictly taboo for any Indian eitlier to enter his motherin-law's apartment, to remain in the same room, to talk with her, or even to look at her.\n\nmother was beginning to feel homesick: anxious to show ofi her husband and child\nto her own people, she told him that they must all leave his place, and go to her\nfather's, up and beyond the clouds. And there they remained with her relations,\nthe Carrion-crows, for many a long day. She, however, was always telling her folk\nwhat a clever man her husband was, and that whatever she asked liim to do, do it\nhe did. So these Crows asked him to perform a number of seemingly impossible\nfeats, and not one did he fail in executing. But this only made all the Crows jealous\nof him, and they determined to put him to death. Makanauxo, being a mediciueman, however, knew that they proposed doing so, and said, \"All right. Let me get\nback to my place, and fetch my friends, and we will fight it out.\" So, taking his\nwife and son, he returned to his old home, and collecting all the birds in the neighborhood, he told them to prepare for the onslaught with the Carrion-crows. Now, when\nthese arrived and saw the hosts of other birds ready to receive them, they determined\nto secure by stratagem a victory which they rect^jiized they could not obtain by\nforce. Their idea was to bum up the whole world, together with Makanauro and\nhis friends in it. For this purpose, the Crows started fires here, there, and everywhere around, but Makanauro saw his friend the black kurri-kurri [Harpiprion\ncayennensis] flying high, and told all his other friends to curse her, he joining in their\nimprecations. This made the rain fall, and so the fires were extinguished.' Now\nthat his wife became angered with him for having frustrated her own people,\nthe Crows, in their design of burning up the world in general, Makanauro left her and\nwent his way. She then sent her son to waylay and kill him, but whether he effected\nthis wicked design I do not know.'\n\n304. In some cases the piais were recognized to a greater or less\nextent as the guardians of the tribal traditions. Thus in the \"Archi-\nT03 de Indias; Patronato. Rodrigo de Navarrete: An account of\nthe Provinces and Nations of the Aruacas\" [Arawaks], written some\ntime during the last quarter of the sixteenth century, a work quoted\nby Rodway, in Timehri (for 1895, p. 10), there is the following interesting reference:\n\nThese Indians have a meeting-place or school where they assemble, as in a manner\nfor preaching. There are among them old and wise men whom they call Cemetu\n[compare the usual form Cemi, Semi, etc.. Sect. 9S]] these assemble in the houses\ndesigned for their meetings and there these old men recount the traditions and exploits\nof their ancestors and great men: and also narrate what those ancestors heard from\ntheir forefathers; so that in this manner they remember the most ancient events\nof their country and people. And, in like manner they recount or preach about\nevents relating to the heavens, the sun, moon, and stars.\n\n305. The medicine-men not only gave names to the children, as\nwith the Arawaks (Sect. 864), but under certain circimistances would\nchange them. Thus, among this same nation, if a piai is called on\nto treat a sick child, and is successful in effecting a cure, he may give\nhis little patient a new name, and thus enable it to make a fresh start\nin life.\n\n306. The chief business, however, of these doctors is centered in\ncounteracting the evil designs of certain Spirits, Kanaima or other,\n\n1 The belief is still prevalent among the Pomeroon Arawaks that if one hears the black kurri-kum\n\"calling \" in early morning, and thereupon curses the bird, rain is certain to fall during the day (Sect. ttS).\n\n) Compare Makona-ura, a youth famous for his skill as a fisher, and credited with invenWng the maswa,\nor fish basket-trap (Da, 259).\n\n346 AinMISM AND FOLK-LOBE OF GtTIANA INDIANS [bth.ann. 30\n\nwho cause disease of such a nature as to baffle the ordinary home\ntreatment and household remedies of the average Indian, though I\nknow of one instance in which a woman in labor was brought by her\nhusband to seek remedial measures from one of this fraternity. The\nhome treatment just referred to might consist in the use of ordinary\nherbs, vapor baths, and in other measures known to the average\nIndian. But occasionally, as with the Dakinis, to obtain such an\nherbal remedy, the piai's assistance may have to be invoked (Sect.\n168B). As a matter of fact, all disease which does not respond\nreadily to treatment is ascribed to various Spirits acting directly or\nindirectly, by means of thorns, pointed bones, etc., maliciously\ninserted into the body of the patient. When once invoked, the medicine-man is able to learn the cause of the trouble, and how to combat\nits effects."

  "passage_text": "307. Disease or death is not a \"natural\" phenomenon, so to speak,\nbut is usually due to one of two agencies. It may be the work\nof some Spirit, perpetrated either judicially or of mere malice, as\nsome affirm, or through the importunity of a votary. An evil\nSpirit, one who causes an evil, might send an animal to bite or sting\na person, or cause a tree to fall upon him, his ax to cut him, water to\ndrown hbn, or some other calamity (Da, 289). Now, except through\nthe agency of the piai, the influence of this Spirit causing the evil can\nnot usually be counteracted. Bennan alone for the Mainland makes\nthe statement, which I must regard as confirmed by the practice\nof a similar custom on the Islands, that \"when sickness assails them,\nthey [laymen. Sect. 89] present a propitiation to the Evil Spirit, consisting of a piece of the flesh of any quadruped. If recovery follows,\nthey suppose the Evil Spirit to have regarded and accepted the offering,\" but if no recovery, the conjurer is called in, etc. (Be, 51-54). The\npiais are undoubtedly believed to have the power of influencing the\nSpirits not only in removing the causes of the disease which they (the\nSpirits) have inflicted, but also in sending sickness elsewhere (Sect. 319) .\nIn the. spring of 1907 the Ojanas (Cayenne) suffered from an epidemic\nof bronchitis, or \"galloping consumption,\" from which many died;\nthis was ascribed to the piais (Go, 14) . It is possible, however, that\nthe medicine-men, independently of Spirits, and certain old people,\ncan inflict sickness on folks at a distance; for instance, the Apalai\nIndians of the upper Parou, Cayenne, when they can not subdue\ntheir sicknesses revenge themselves by sending an evil charm to a\nwoman (Sect. 319) of the neighboring tribe (Cr, 299). It is not at\nall uncommon for one tribe to put the blame of some real or imagined\niU on the shoulders of another. For example, the Wapisianas consider the Makusis the most dangerous poisoners and Kanaimas —\nevery ilbaess is ascribed by them to the wickedness of the Makusis\n(ScE, II, 387). Similarly, on the Tiquie River (Rio Negro) theMakua\n\nare blamed for everything (KG, i, 270) . There is a certain skin disease,\nbelieved to be a vitiligo, which the Piapocos of the lower Guaviar\n(Orinoco River) call sero: it is always contracted by drinking the\nyocrtto (fiouac mixed with water) of an enemy aflFected with this\ntrouble, who has mixed in the brew a few drops of his blood (Cr, 527).\nDeath and other evils may be due also to some human enemy more\nor less disguised, modified, or influenced by a peculiarly terrible Spirit\nknown as Kanaima, against whose machinations the power of the\npiai avails nothing. To this belief in Kanaima I propose devoting a\nseparate chapter (Sect. 320).\n\n308. In the Pomeroon District, the present-day Arawak procedure\nof the piai, for the treatment of disease, is as follows : Suppose the\npatient visits the \"doctor,\" the latter will sling the sufferer's hammock in the special out-house already mentioned. In those cases\nin which the person is too ill to bear removal, the doctor will visit\nhim, and there erect a closely plaited conical-shaped cage of manicole leaves, with a low door only just large enough to crawl in and\nout by. Nothing further can be done now until the sun sets, but\nas soon after sundown as convenient the medicine-man will start\na new fire, by twirling one stick upon another. The fire once kindled,\nhe rolls tobacco to make the usual Indian cigarette, and proceeds to\nexamine the patient. He then asks what the pain is Uke, and where\nit is — as, in stomach, head, chest, — and talks to his kickshaws, especially the manikin, or doll, to learn whether the patient is going to\nbe cured. The method of employment of this doll has already\nbeen given (Sect. 290). Seated on his special chair, the doctor next\nlights and smokes his cigarette, and finally rubs his hands with\nhaiawa wax. This done, he proceeds to massage the painful spot,\nand smokes on it through his hands placed funnel-wise. This part\nof the treatment may be viewed by the pubUc, there being nothing\nsecret or mysterious about it, and may of itself effect a cure, in which\ncase, as the Creoles would say, \"Story done.\" With the next procedure, however, provided the iUness prove stubborn, the females are\nall sent away from the place, men have to keep at a respectful distance,\nquiet must reign, and all fights have to be extinguished. The alleged\nreason for putting out the fires is that the various Spirits whom he is\nnow about to invoke may not be afraid to come. (If the treatment\nis being carried out at the patient's residence, the medicine-man will\ncrawl into the cage when the invocation takes place.) In the meantime, the medicine-man cleans and polishes his maraka, which he\npieces together, and ties the feathers carefidly on, smoking on it aU\nthe while: he sings and shakes his rattle. Leaving his bench, he\ntouches the painful spot or spots with the maraka, circling it in the\nair, smoking and singing all the while, altering his voice from bass to\nalto and vice-versa according to the voice of the Spirit which is pre-\n\n348 ANIMISM AND FOLK-LOEE OF GUIANA INDIANS [eth. ann. 30"
}

Our medicine-man,\nseated on his divining stool, will proceed to smoke and dream, and\nin his dream he will discover at whose instigation the sickness has\nbeen sent, and whether the illness itself is due to a dead person's\nSpirit (as a Bush Spirit) , to a living one's Spirit (a Kanaima), or to the\nOriyu, or Water Spirit. At the same time he also learns the mode of\ncure. Next morning he will retail this information either to the\npatient or to his friends, as soon as he is paid something over and\nabove the fee (as cloth, beads, money), which he has already received.\nThe cure may be such as can then and there be carried out, as the\nextraction of the evil by suction, or the disease may prove of so\nserious a nature that it is a matter for the Spirits alone to deal with.\nAt any rate the medicine-man then gives careful directions as to how\nthe patient and his relatives are to be fed — ^with bird, fish, or otherwise,\nas the case may be — but there is always the stipulation that whatever\nis ordered (a) must never be added to, or taken away from, for\nexample, no salt, peppers, seasoning, etc., and no \"trimming off;\"\n(6) must be cooked with the doctor's own fire, or with another\nspecially made for the purpose by means of two pieces of stick, care\nbeing taken in both cases that it is not touched by a stranger; (c) must\nnot be allowed to boil over the edge of the pot. If during the course\nof the day the patient should not improve, the doctor will repeat the\ntreatment the same night — smoking, singing, and dreaming — ^but on\nthis occasion, addressing the Spirit which has caused the mischief,\nhe implores it if possible to restore the health which it has impaired.\nHe may even repeat all this the third night if the patient's grave\ncondition warrants so doing, and he is paid an adequate fee. At any\nrate, when he finally completes the treatment the doctor invariably\ntells the patient, unless the latter is actually moribund, that he wiU\nrecover, but that both he and his family must be very careful as to\nthe foods prescribed, for should the sufferer unfortunately die it is\nalways because one or other of the stipulations regarding diet has\nnot been properly obeyed. Among the Pomeroon Caribs I have been present on several\noccasions on the Manawarin River at the procedure adopted by a piai\nto aflfect a cure. It has always been at night, with the doctor seated in\na small temporary cone-shaped structure roughly made of manicole\nleaves, and the rattle brought into requisition. If the disease has been sent by one\nor other of these bad Spirits, the piai gets Mawari to take it far, far\naway, away to the Orinoco River; but if by another piai, the present\ncelebrant will send it back to him, and woe betide the latter if he is not\nsmart enough to avoid it, for unless he takes very great care he is\nsure to die from it. But if Tiger should prove\nunsuccessful, nothing now can possibly save the patient."

  "passage_text": "310. The Gahbi piai of French Guiana practised similar methods, '
according to the accounts left us by Barrere: After placing the
maraka below the patient's hammock, the piai starts sucking at
those parts of the sick person's body where the pains are greatest,
afterward passing both hands over the patient; he then strikes his
hands together and blows on each palm (Sect. 85) so as to drive
away the "Devil" [Spirit] that has attached itself there (Sect. 74)',
the piai wiU sometimes pinch up pieces of his own skin, and thus
extracting corpulency (embonpoint) and good health, will apply
these in handsful to the patient while making the passes over him.

350 ASriMISM AND FOLK-LOEE OF GUIANA INDIANS [bth. ann. 30

These Indians also employed the little hut specially constructed in
the Tcarbet, in which, after all the lights have been extinguished, the
medicine-men "sings" and shakes the rattle. He often comes out of
his Httle cabin and would pretend that it is the Devil [Spirit] that has
got out. He will then run right round the Tcarbet and tug at the
hammocks in which the Indians are lying. He sometimes says that
he is going up into the skies, but will soon return, and he wiU then
mimic the distant voice, etc. (PBa, 213-215).

311. In remote parts [of French Guiana] and toward the sources of
the River Oyapok, the Indians [ ? Oyampis] practise another method,
with the figure of a Devil [Spirit] made of a very soft and resonant
wood. This statue, which is three or four feet high, looks frightful,
with its long tail (queue) and big claws with which they provide it.
They call it Anaan-tanha (literally, Devil-figure). After having
blown on the sick person, the piais carry the statue out of the hut.
There they talk to it, and thrash it unmercifully with sticks, so as to
force the Devil [Spirit], in spite of itself, to leave the sick person. These
exorcisms are carried out at night, after the fires have been extinguished (PBa, 216). Very interesting in this connection is the maizestraw manikin, found by Cr6vaux, among the Apalai Indians of
Cayenne (Cr, 301), which may have been employed for a simiilar
purpose; it represented a warrior ready to let fly an arrow, fixed on
two sticks arranged crosswise like a gallows.

312. It is not always necessary, however, to use the maraka, it
being quite possible to invoke the Spirits with a couple of bundles
of leaves. Thus, Schomburgk gives the following account of a
Makusi performance at Nappi, on the Canuku Mountains:

The old man came into my hut with two bundles of leaves in his hands, and with
them he drove out the other occ upanta . He then put out al 1 the fires, sat near my hammock on the ground, which he whipped with the bundles, and started howling, only
now and again broken by short pauses. After this had gone on for a quarter of an hour,
I recognized a second voice by the side of my hammock, and question and answer went
on between the two. The conversations with the evil spirits are unintelligible even
to the Indians: it was next morning that the piai took care to make them aware of its
contents. After the double conversation was finished, the magician placed himself
at the head-end of my hammock, howled close to my forehead and, after lighting a
cigar, blew strong clouds of tobacco-smoke into my face which almost suffocated me,
and pressed the bundle of leaves (which I recognized by the smell as tobacco leaves)
onto my forehead. This went on for quite half an hour and got me into a good sweat:
at last his voice failed him, and he left the hut. He did not use the maraka. [ScR
II, 145-146.] '

313. Westward of the Guianas a particular kind of wood apparently
played the same r61e as the rattle or the leaf-bundle, if we accept the
statement of Depons in his description of the Captain Generalship of
Caracas:

The practice of these professors of the healing art consisted in licking and sucking
the affected part, in order, according to them, to eliminate the peccant humour.

When the fever or pain increased, suction of the joints, as well as friction over all the
body with the hand, was employed. During the performance of this operation,
some unintelligible words were pronounced, with a loud voice, commanding the evil
spirits to depart out of the patient's body. If the malady did not readily yield, the
Piache or physician had recourse to a particular kind of wood, known to himself
alone, with which he rubbed the breast, throat, and mouth of the patient; a practice
which seldom foiled to produce sickness and vomiting. In the meantime the Piache
on his side uttered dreadful exclamations, howled, shook, and made a thousand contortions with his body. If the sick person recovered, everything contained in the house
was given to the Piache; if he died, the fault was imputed to Destiny, never to the
physician. [FD, 50.]

314. Among the Island Carib Indians the piai procedure was of
the simplest kind :

They say that the Chemeen [Sect. 90 et seq.] always comes on scenting the odor of
this incense [tobacco] and, being interrt^ated, he answers with a clear voice, but
sounding as from a distance. The sorcerer then approaches the sick person repeatedly,
feels, presses, and manipulates the suffering part, always blowing on it, and extracts
something from it, or rather appears to extract, some thorns, or small pieces of cassava,
wood, or bones, making the sick person believe that this was the sole cause of the pain.
Very often he sucks the painful part, and immediately goes out of the house to vomit
what he calls the poison. [BBR, 234.]

They also moisten with their\nbreath the weak spot and having repeatedly sucked it, they persuade the patient\nthat by this means they have extracted the poison which was in his body and kept it\nin languor. They finally rub the sick person's body with junipa fruit. . . But\nif the Boye has learnt from the communication which he has had with his demon\nthat the sickness is a fatal one, he contents himself with consoling the sick person by\nthe statement that this God, or rather to say, his Familiar Devil, having pity on him,\nwishes to take him into his company, so as to be freed from all his infirmities. [RoP,\n564.]\n\n315. \"With regard to the nature of the Spirits specially invoked,\nBarrington Brown (Bro, 140) when describing the performances of a\nMakusi piai at Mora Village, upper Rupununi, remarks that —\n\nIn some instances the good spirit for the time being brought with it the evil one\nthat was supposed to have had some hand in producing the man's malady; and then\nthe wife asked it how it could come and injure a being who had never harmed it,\nbegging it to desist and leave her husband alone. The only answer she obtained to\nthis appeal was a most diabolical, mocking laugh. The llakunaima, or great spirit.\n\n352 ' ANIMISM AND FOLK-LOEB OF GXJIANA INDIANS [kth. ANN. SO\n\nwas never called upon by the sorcerer to assist or cure the sick man, but only the subordinate inhabitants of spirit-land.'\n\n316. The last-mentioned is very interesting in view of the\nArawak Indians' behef (Br, 361) that all pain is due to the Evil\nSpirit's arrow (Sect. SSO). The medicos of the Otomac nation suck\nwith such force as to extract blood from the patient, and when this\nis spat out on a cleared space, minute stony particles are to be seen\nin it (G, II, 27).
